articles.title: Kai extends Autonomous Defense Platform visibility to internet-facing assets
articles.context: Kai has announced External Attack Surface Management (EASM), now available on the Kai Autonomous Defense Platform
articles.full_text:
Kai has announced External Attack Surface Management (EASM), now available on the Kai Autonomous Defense Platform. The company also launched Kai Labs, an expanded research team focused on the hardest open problems where AI meets security.

Most exposure management programs only see inside, so they miss the exposures attackers find first. With EASM, Kai unifies internal and external exposures into a single remediation plan, accelerating the path to zero. The external view sharpens what counts as real risk and lets teams address exposures comprehensively from one platform.

“Attackers start outside, and for most organizations the outside is the part they understand least,” said Dr. Damiano Bolzoni, CTO of Kai. “Extending our platform to the external attack surface means teams see their exposure the way an attacker does and fix it in the same place they manage everything else.”

Kai unifies internal and external exposures into a single remediation plan

Many teams manage external and internal exposure with different tools, and the data from each is not integrated. Analysts reconcile external findings with internal data by hand to determine ownership, risk, and priority, which slows security down.

With EASM, Kai brings both surfaces into one platform and a single dataset, so external and internal exposure can be analyzed together at machine speed. The result is a clearer view of which exposures are real risk and single plan to close them. That matters because the external attack surface changes every day: new cloud services, forgotten subsidiaries, test sites left online, and APIs and AI services stood up without a security review.

Key capabilities include:

Discovery and attribution: Discovers the internet-facing assets tied to an organization’s domains, including assets that CMDBs and internal asset inventories commonly miss.

Exposed AI infrastructure: Finds LLM endpoints, MCP servers, and vector databases.

API visibility: Breaks published API definitions down into the individual endpoints they expose.

Attacker-style investigation: Investigates and uncovers exposures the same way an attacker would.

One asset record, one queue: Every external exposure joins the same asset record, aligns to the same owners, and is fixed through the same workflow as internal vulnerabilities and misconfigurations.

Introducing Kai Labs

Alongside EASM, Kai is launching Kai Labs, an expanded research team that tackles the hardest open problems where AI meets security. Kai Labs tests its ideas in real security programs, not just the lab.

Kai Labs is led by Kylie McClanahan, PhD, Research Director, whose career spans vulnerability management, prioritization, and remediation. The team pairs AI scientists with security researchers in detection, application security, offensive research, and AI red teaming.

Its first research areas are offensive learning, autonomous action, decision models, trusted autonomy, and security context, spanning how AI attackers learn, how fixes are generated and verified, and how defenders can trust autonomous action. Kai Labs publishes its findings through blogs, conference talks, and peer-reviewed papers.

articles.title: Rubrik enhances DevOps Protection to preserve legitimate work during recovery
articles.context: ” Attackers no longer need to breach perimeters; instead, they compromise legitimate credentials to launch attacks that mimic normal developer activity
articles.full_text:
Rubrik has announced cyber recovery capabilities for DevOps platforms Microsoft Azure DevOps and GitHub. With built-in anomaly detection, blast radius investigation, and surgical recovery, organizations will be able to detect suspicious activity on their code, instantly scope the impact of an attack, and undo the attackers’ changes from air-gapped, immutable backups, without disrupting legitimate developer work.

“An organization’s source code is where innovation lives, and attackers know it,” said Anneka Gupta, Chief Product Officer at Rubrik. “One stolen token or poisoned dependency can impact thousands of repositories before anyone notices. Our new cyber recovery capabilities for DevOps allow organizations to detect suspicious activity, see what was impacted, and recover only the unwanted changes, using the air-gapped backups they already trust Rubrik to protect.”

Attackers no longer need to breach perimeters; instead, they compromise legitimate credentials to launch attacks that mimic normal developer activity. Accelerated by AI, these attacks can rapidly spread malicious code across thousands of repositories.

According to Gartner, “a growing number of software engineering leaders are modernizing their DevSecOps toolchains by adopting DevSecOps platforms.” These platforms house an organization’s most critical intellectual property, including source code, CI/CD pipelines, and infrastructure as code. As such, they’ve become a primary, identity-driven attack surface.

Enhanced DevOps Protection capabilities

Operating natively within Rubrik Security Cloud, DevOps Protection Enterprise Edition now connects detection, investigation, and recovery in a single workflow:

Anomaly detection: Continuously baselines GitHub and Azure DevOps audit logs, correlating them with Rubrik backup metadata to flag suspicious identity activity and produce a prioritized alert that can be routed directly into existing security and ticketing workflows.

Blast radius investigation: Produces a categorized view of affected assets across repositories, commits, pipelines, workflows, pull requests, and settings, providing the exact scope of impact and determining precisely what needs to be restored.

Surgical recovery: Recovers only what the attacker changed while preserving legitimate work from other developers, using the clean, air-gapped, immutable backups customers already hold with Rubrik DevOps Protection. Teams will be able to avoid manual rebuilds and organization-wide code freezes.

Expanded developer collaboration stack protection

To ensure complete recovery context, Rubrik DevOps Protection (Foundation Edition) now backs up broader platform metadata, settings, and the developer collaboration stack across Azure DevOps and GitHub. From issues, pull requests, and Azure Boards to wikis, packages, and organization settings, businesses can recover the full context of how their teams build software, rather than just the underlying code.

Rubrik’s cyber recovery capabilities for DevOps platforms Microsoft Azure DevOps and GitHub is expected to be generally available in the coming months.

articles.title: Orca Security adds visibility into AI-generated code and agent risks
articles.context: Expand security coverage across AI development platforms: Turn discovered services into actionable security coverage through supported integrations and posture assessments,...
articles.full_text:
Orca Security has announced new capabilities to help organizations discover and secure AI-generated applications and autonomous agents across their cloud environments. The expansion builds on Orca’s AI Security offering, enabling security teams to uncover previously unknown AI applications, assess the risks associated with autonomous agents, and gain deeper visibility into AI-generated code.

AI is fundamentally changing who builds software and how it reaches production. Employees across business functions are creating applications using AI-powered tools, while developers increasingly rely on autonomous agents to write code and execute tasks. Yet many of these applications and agents operate outside traditional security processes, creating new blind spots.

“AI has turned everyone into a builder, but security teams are often the last to know what’s been created,” said Gil Geron, CEO of Orca Security. “An employee can deploy an application over the weekend, while an autonomous agent can access sensitive data and take actions across cloud environments. Organizations need to understand not just what exists, but what it can access and where it creates risk. We’re bringing that context to the entire AI development ecosystem so companies can keep innovating without losing control.”

Uncovering shadow AI applications through digital fingerprints

As employees increasingly use AI development platforms such as Lovable, Replit, and Bolt to create applications outside traditional engineering workflows, security teams often lack visibility into what has been deployed, where it runs, or what company data it can access. Traditional discovery approaches depend on knowing which platforms, applications, or repositories to monitor, leaving unknown AI-generated applications undetected.

Orca’s expanded AI AppGen Security capabilities address this challenge by identifying digital fingerprints that AI application builders leave behind across cloud infrastructure, DNS records, workloads, code repositories, and cloud identities. Using its patented agentless SideScanning technology and unified data model, Orca connects these signals to uncover previously unknown AI services without requiring additional agents, vendor integrations, or employee registration.

New capabilities allow users to:

Discover shadow AI applications through service fingerprints: Automatically detect digital fingerprints left behind by AI application builders such as Lovable, v0, Replit, Base44, and Bolt, alongside hosting and data services including Vercel, Netlify, and Supabase. Orca identifies evidence such as DNS records pointing to builder infrastructure, installed packages, file markers, AI builder commit identities, and cloud permissions, revealing services that security teams may not know are in use.

Connect fingerprints to business risk: Correlate discovered services with cloud identities, IAM permissions, and accessible resources to help security teams understand which AI-generated applications may have access to sensitive company data. Findings are presented through a dedicated Service Fingerprints view, asset-level details, and an AI AppGen dashboard, providing the evidence behind each discovery.

Expand security coverage across AI development platforms: Turn discovered services into actionable security coverage through supported integrations and posture assessments, including checks for insecure configurations such as disabled row-level security in Supabase projects. Orca is also extending AI AppGen Security support to Base44, OpenAI, and Vercel.

“Many organizations still struggle to discover what’s been built and where it runs. Now that building is no longer confined to engineering, discovery has to start from what these AI-generated apps leave behind in the environment, not from the builder declaring anything,” said Grace Trinidad, Research Director, IDC.

Securing autonomous AI agents and AI-generated code

Beyond AI-generated applications, autonomous agents introduce a new category of security risk. Unlike traditional AI models, agents can execute commands, access sensitive information, and interact with enterprise systems using the credentials and permissions available to them. A single overprivileged agent or insecure connection can create a path to sensitive data or critical infrastructure.

Orca’s expanded AI agent security posture capabilities provide visibility into cloud-managed and self-hosted agents, including coding agents operating on cloud infrastructure. By incorporating agents into its unified data model and existing cloud security workflows, Orca enables organizations to:

Discover and inventory AI agents: Automatically identify cloud-managed and self-hosted agents, including coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex, and Gemini CLI running on cloud workloads. A new Agents tab in Orca’s AI Bill of Materials (AIBOM) provides a centralized inventory alongside AI models, packages, and MCP servers, with filtering by cloud, account, and framework.

Map agent relationships and access: Connect agents to the AI models they use, MCP servers and tools they interact with, cloud identities they operate under, and data stores they can access. This context helps security teams understand an agent’s potential blast radius and identify paths to sensitive data.

Detect and prioritize agent-specific risks: Identify agents with excessive permissions, disabled approval controls, exposed credentials in MCP configurations, insecure HTTP connections, or access to destructive tools. Findings are incorporated into Orca’s dynamic risk scoring and attack path analysis to prioritize the most consequential exposures and provide actionable remediation guidance.

Track and secure AI-generated code: Attribute code to the coding agents and AI models that produced it, helping organizations understand the proportion of AI-generated code across repositories and identify which agents and models contribute the most security risk. Through Orca’s AI Skills Hub, developers can also integrate security requirements, application security scanning, and remediation directly into coding agents before code is committed.

These capabilities extend Orca’s existing cloud security workflows to AI agents, enabling organizations to assess agent-related risks alongside vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, identities, and sensitive data across their environments.

articles.title: Commvault rolls out an automated recovery mechanism, promising faster restoration of business
articles.context: ” The news release said that the new application can deliver other cybersecurity assistance via data security checks, including “automated threat scanning for supported...
articles.full_text:
Commvault on Tuesday rolled out its answer to enterprise backup restoration nightmares. Called Recovery Studio, the vendor promised that the product would “orchestrate the recovery of applications, identities, configurations, infrastructure dependencies, and datasets together in an automated, runbook-driven workflow.”

Analysts and consultants applauded the effort, agreeing that enterprises today struggle with fast, accurate and secure restorations. But they also stressed that the new system, which is targeted for early access in December with general availability “in the coming months,” places the onus on IT to keep a dependency map current.

Recovery Studio isn’t using any form of AI to figure out proper restoration details. It relies on a map of assets, dependencies, and other relevant information that the customer creates and maintains, and for many enterprises, the challenge of keeping such a document current is the real problem. Even discounting the times when a line of business doesn’t tell IT about an application change, IT teams struggle to keep up with the speed of change in the organization.

Commvault’s news release said that its automation allows businesses to “say goodbye to manual and painstaking attempts to restore complicated business services in a fragmented fashion that can result in downtime and data loss.”

It pointed out that a large enterprise may need to restore hundreds of applications and thousands of identities, including the configurations and underlying data, all in the right order at the right time. “It’s no wonder that with conventional approaches, recovery to even a minimal level of operation takes an average of 28 days,” the release said.

Commvault said Recovery Studio can manage a wide range of components that go beyond containers, VMs, files, and objects, extending to identity systems, application configurations, infrastructure configurations and security and network settings.

It also promised that the Recovery Studio can standardize “across all recovery scenarios” including “operational, disaster and cyber recoveries. Unified runbooks automate infrastructure rebuilds, workload recovery, and the orchestration of security controls, such as firewall rules and network security groups and settings – all actions needed to rebuild the business, not just recover data.”

The news release said that the new application can deliver other cybersecurity assistance via data security checks, including “automated threat scanning for supported resources in the runbook to identify compromised areas and inform recovery decisions before returning services to production.”

Commvault did not provide a spokesperson to offer further details before publication.

Depends on IT awareness of the environment

A number of factors will influence the effectiveness of the solution, analysts said.

Frank Dickson, principal analyst at Dickson Research, pointed out, “nothing in Commvault’s announcement describes a generative model making recovery decisions. This is runbook automation. A runbook is a recipe: do this, then this, then this. It does not hallucinate. It does exactly what it is told.”

“That is the real risk. A flawed runbook gets executed flawlessly, at machine speed,” he said. “Automation does not make a bad plan good. It makes a bad plan fast.”

That means, said Aman Mahapatra, chief strategy officer for New York City-based technology consulting firm Tribeca Softech, whether Recovery Studio ultimately helps or hurts enterprise restoration efforts depends on how aware IT is of everything going on in its global footprint.

“How much it solves depends on something no vendor controls, which is the accuracy of the dependency map underneath it. A runbook is a prediction about your environment and every change since it was last tested makes it a little more wrong: a new application, a rotated certificate, a firewall rule added on a Friday,” Mahapatra said.

“Most enterprise dependency maps are aspirational,” he noted, “and CMDBs in particular tend to describe the environment someone intended to build. Commvault’s figure of 28 days to reach minimal operations is plausible, but the gains will go to organizations that refresh and rehearse their runbooks continuously. For everyone else, automation will execute an outdated plan faster.”

Abbas Jaffery, principal advisory director at Infotech, agreed.

“My concern is that automation can execute the wrong recovery sequence just as efficiently as the right one. Enterprise environments change constantly,” Jaffery said. “Applications are upgraded, infrastructure moves, identities change and integrations are added or removed. If the dependency information behind a recovery workflow is outdated, automation could restore systems successfully but leave the business service broken.”

Defined recovery

Mike Leone, a VP and principal analyst at Moor Insights & Strategy, added that Commvault is still advancing the space.

Recovery Studio “follows defined recovery runbooks rather than a model inventing steps on the fly. That’s much more deterministic and structured,” Leone said. “Sure, automation can repeat a mistake faster than a person can, and a runbook that’s gone stale is a fair concern. But Commvault is validating each piece as it rebuilds and scanning for threats before anything goes back into production. Those are the kind of safeguards and checks everyone should want. The alternative is people rebuilding systems by hand in the middle of an outage, and that isn’t exactly mistake-free either.”

But Dickson stressed that automation is not necessarily the perfect fix.

“Commvault says the runbooks validate components and can scan supported resources for threats before services return to production. Good,” he said. “But the honest comparison is not automation versus perfection. It is automation versus exhausted people working from a spreadsheet at 3 a.m. Humans get the order wrong, too.”

Johnny Yu, an IDC research manager, is not as impressed by the components of the solution as he is by the way Recovery Studio organizes them.

“I do see Commvault Recovery Studio as significant, but not from a capability standpoint,” Yu said, adding that all of the product’s components, including recovery runbooks, threat scans, and recovery testing, are already offered by Commvault, as well as by various competitors. “I think the significance comes from how Recovery Studio organizes different recovery workflows for different applications onto a single platform or hub, kind of like a library of validated recovery runbooks to be used for all kinds of scenarios.”

He explained that he liked how Studio standardizes recovery runbooks to follow a similar workflow to that of manually rebuilding the environment, recovering the components, such as data, applications and agents, and “validating the recovery before bringing it back into production, but allows recovery nuance for each runbook, such as if you want to do in-place vs secondary-site recovery or whether threat scanning is necessary, such as DR scenario vs cyber recovery scenario.”

Jaffery noted, however, that while the promised Commvault cybersecurity controls are attractive, they may also be insufficient.

“Following a cyberattack, organizations need to be confident they aren’t restoring compromised identities, configurations or malicious persistence mechanisms,” Jaffery said. “I would not advocate fully autonomous recovery for every scenario. There needs to be appropriate human authorization for high-impact actions, particularly those involving identity, security controls and reconnecting systems to production. And organizations need to test the entire recovery process, not just whether the backup can be restored.”

An AI agent recovery plan

Commvault on Tuesday also introduced AgentRecover capabilities to help track and control autonomous agents. It would specifically “help organizations audit agent activity, restore agents, and recover the data and systems they affected across environments.”

Mahapatra noted that AgentRecover addresses a potentially more difficult problem than system restorations.

“Restoring an agent’s configuration is straightforward. Unwinding what it did is not, because an agent’s actions land as side effects in other systems, and some of them, such as an email sent or a payment initiated, cannot be restored at all,” Mahapatra said.

“Traditional recovery rolls back to a point in time,” he explained. “Rolling an environment back to 9 a.m. erases everyone’s legitimate work since 9 a.m., while rolling back only what the agent changed requires knowing causality: which agent, acting under which identity, changed which record. Commvault’s mapping of agent activity and the identities agents act through points in the right direction.”

Jaffery added that rollbacks of an autonomous agent can be especially daunting.

“Restoring the agent itself doesn’t necessarily undo what it has done. An agent might modify customer records, change permissions, invoke APIs or trigger downstream transactions,” he said. “You need to understand what actions it performed and what the consequences were before deciding what to reverse or restore.”

Leone also noted that agents can complicate system restoration, partially because of their speed.

“Agents don’t wait for anyone to confirm things are safe. The moment a system comes back, agents start hitting it, far faster than any person would,” he said. “If an agent comes back before the data and identities it relies on are verified, it starts acting on stale or incomplete information at machine speed. Get the order wrong and one outage quickly turns into a second one.”

Jaffery also observed that Commvault is far from alone in the automated restoration space, and may even be a tad late.

“I don’t think Commvault has an uncontested position here. Rubrik, Cohesity and Veeam have all been investing in cyber recovery, application recovery and orchestration,” he said. “Rubrik, in particular, has been pushing toward automated business application recovery and dependency mapping. Cohesity has capabilities around cyber recovery orchestration and cloud application reconstruction, while Veeam has an established disaster recovery orchestration offering.”

articles.title: Cisco Unveils Frontier AI Red Teaming and Agent Observability to Secure the Agentic Enterprise
articles.context:
Cisco innovations offer enterprises an always-on trust loop to secure, govern, and observe increasingly capable AI agents and complex enterprise AI deployments.

articles.full_text:
News Summary:

Cisco AI Defense's adaptive AI red teaming framework is adding Anthropic's Claude Mythos, harnessing advanced adversarial reasoning to simulate real-world attacks on AI agents.

With Cisco’s enhanced Tokenomics, organizations can optimize AI spend to defend what matters most by connecting agent cost directly with ROI in real time.

Cisco IQ, which leverages decades of vulnerability and troubleshooting data, now correlates live threat detection data with potentially exposed network infrastructure at machine speed to accelerate remediation.

Together, these innovations offer enterprises an always-on trust loop to secure, govern, and observe increasingly capable AI agents and complex enterprise AI deployments.

MELBOURNE, Australia, Nov. 10, 2026 -- CISCO LIVE APJC -- Cisco (NASDAQ: CSCO) today announced it is adding Claude Mythos to AI Defense for red teaming AI applications and agents, empowering defenders to stress-test AI systems with frontier adversary reasoning. Coupled with new Splunk Agent Observability and Cisco IQ advancements, Cisco is preparing enterprises for a new era of trust that requires securing, observing, and governing agents at machine speed.

“You cannot scale what you cannot secure, govern, or observe,” said Cisco President and Chief Product Officer Jeetu Patel. “By uniting frontier-level AI runtime protections with machine-speed agent quality controls, we are building a continuous trust loop: protecting agents from compromise while ensuring every token spent delivers measurable business value.”

As AI agents proliferate and connect to complex tools and sensitive data, 81% of ITOps and engineering professionals cite increased cooperation between security and observability teams, according to a global Splunk research report last month. Cisco’s Splunk and AI Defense innovations equip security leaders to account for token spend and effective tool use while conducting tailored security testing against highly capable AI agents.

Since Cisco launched AI Defense in January 2025, it has helped hundreds of customers identify critical flaws in AI models, applications, and agents before they reach production. Its adaptive red teaming allows security teams to quickly build customized, multi-step attacks on target systems to uncover specific risks. Claude Mythos will augment this framework with advanced reasoning that plans tests that matter and translates the results into attack ideas for each system.

Features include:

Realistic Adversarial Ideation: generates multi-step, contextual attack paths designed to help identify subtle vulnerabilities across complex architectures.

Secure, Contained Access: By design, customers interact only through AI Defense's structured interface: Customers have no open-ended prompt access.

Audit Trails and Repeatable Results: AI Defense records each testing action for audit, and results can be carried over to inform follow-up attack loops.

“Enterprises are increasingly building AI agents into their core operations and want to test those agents thoroughly before putting them into production,” said Michael Moore, Cybersecurity Lead at Anthropic. “By bringing Claude Mythos to Cisco AI Defense, Cisco can help security teams red team their agents with advanced reasoning that plans tests and generates attack ideas for each system.”

Cisco engineered AI Defense to use Claude Mythos with multi-layered safeguards:

Registered, Authorized Targets: Operates exclusively against targets explicitly registered, owned, and authorized for testing by the enterprise customer; it cannot scan arbitrary internet infrastructure.

Named Operator Attribution: Every red teaming engagement requires authentication and is cryptographically tied to a named enterprise operator.

Revocable Execution: Engagements run with a fixed job and objectives defined by the human user, with time-bound sessions that can be halted on demand.

Dual-Layer Oversight: Product-level controls in AI Defense operate alongside program-level safeguards and monitoring.

Closing the Loop: From Test Findings to Measurable Agent ROI

Frontier AI models can excel at complex security tasks such as crafting AI red teaming strategies. That capability cuts both ways. AI is lowering the barrier to entry for attackers just as many enterprises are working to balance security, governance, and ROI considerations across growing AI portfolios.

For organizations to confidently deploy AI agents at scale, they need unified, real-time visibility into AI agent cost, business performance, and quality. Cisco is bridging the trust gap with new Splunk Agent Observability enhancements:

Tokenomics: cost governance, soon to be available in AWS Marketplace, that ties AI spend to output quality. Using usage data from Amazon Bedrock and Amazon CloudWatch, it pairs each agent's cost with evaluations that grade the quality and impact of its work, giving organizations a single view of AI ROI. This extends the token-spend attribution launched at .conf26, which tracks costs across AI agents and coding tools such as Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor.

Eval-G1 Evaluation Models: Splunk Agent Observability extends our support for turning agentic traces and expert feedback into custom small language models that execute evals and guardrails at up to 98% lower cost than a commercial LLM. These next generation Eval-G1 models deliver evaluation response times 2.5x faster than traditional LLMs and enable real-time agent control with high accuracy.

The Evaluation Tuner: Teams can turn their agentic traces and subject matter expert feedback into fine-tuned evaluator models to enforce quality standards and steer agents at machine speed.

Adaptive red teaming with Claude Mythos is coming soon for select enterprises. Tokenomics will be available in private preview in December, with general availability in AWS Marketplace early 2027. The evaluation models and the evaluation tuner are generally available starting this month.

Connecting Infrastructure Exposure to Security Action with Cisco IQ and Cisco Data Fabric Powered by the Splunk Platform

While understanding vulnerability exposure is critical, defenders must also accelerate how they remediate risk across complex enterprise estates. Cisco IQ identifies critical exposures, and the powerful ecosystem of Cisco Partners and Professional Services turns insight into action. Partners help deliver remediation at scale and modernize infrastructure, and Cisco Professional Services bring deep expertise to put new Cisco capabilities into practice. Together, Cisco and its partners can help streamline operations and future-proof your IT infrastructure for the AI era.

As AI-accelerated threats compress the window between vulnerability disclosure and exploitation from weeks to hours, point-in-time audits leave organizations exposed. To help security and network operations teams act at machine speed, Cisco is extending real-time intelligence from Cisco IQ—which has close to 17,000 customers across more than 22 million devices—directly into enterprise security environments, open agentic protocols, and automated lifecycle workflows.

Key updates include:

Cisco Data Fabric Integration: Ingests Cisco IQ vulnerability, lifecycle, and configuration data directly into Splunk Platform via open APIs, enabling SecOps teams and AI agents to correlate live threat detections with underlying network exposure in Splunk Enterprise Security.

Model Context Protocol (MCP) & ServiceNow Connectors: Provides structured infrastructure context to supported AI agents and enterprise IT Service Management platforms, automatically translating exposure findings into asset-linked ServiceNow problem records to coordinate remediation without manual data reconciliation.

AI-Powered Resilient Infrastructure Playbook: Surfaces critical lifecycle vulnerabilities, including personalized alerts for known defects and quantum-safe cryptographic readiness, allowing teams and certified partners to scope and prioritize modernization roadmaps.

“AI is shrinking the time organizations have to respond to threats, and knowing where you're exposed only matters if you can act on it,” said Liz Centoni, Cisco EVP and Chief Customer Experience Officer. “Bringing Cisco IQ vulnerability insights into Cisco Data Fabric powered by the Splunk Platform gives analysts that context in the middle of an investigation, so they can decide what to do next. With our partners and Professional Services teams, we're helping customers move from identifying risk to actually reducing it.”

To learn more about securing and observing the agentic enterprise, visit cisco.com/go/ai-defense.

Though many look to ensure that they meet mission readiness requirements, overreliance on these practices can allow hidden risks to go unchecked.

Host Maria Varmazis sits down with ⁠Vito Askins⁠, founder of ⁠Green Until Integration Consulting⁠, to discuss risk accumulation and operational readiness. The two look at how these integration risk can often go overlooking during systems integration monitoring efforts.

In this article

Mitigation and protection guidance

Microsoft Defender detections

Hunting queries

Indicators of compromise

In October 2026, the financially motivated threat actor Storm-3358 began targeting organizations in the financial sector using the agentic AI offensive framework ARTEX. The threat actor that Microsoft Threat Intelligence tracks as Storm-3358 is a Cambodia-based intrusion cluster that primarily targets financial organizations in Southeast Asia, in addition to a smaller number of large financial organizations globally.

Microsoft has observed Storm-3358 use ARTEX in combination with conventional automated tools to scan systems connected to the public internet, exploit security flaws including anonymous file upload and server-side request forgery (SSRF), and install open-source remote access trojans (RATs). Storm-3358 has used the WISP, vshell, and AdaptixC2 RATs for persistence and lateral movement. Microsoft has observed ARTEX agents using utilities like netcat and curl to download these RATs to compromised systems, as shown in Figure 1.

Figure 1. Example commands that ARTEX agents used to download RATs to compromised systems.

In recent ARTEX-related attacks, threat actors have used ARTEX agents to scan and exploit vulnerabilities in web applications, use web shells for persistence on compromised web servers, compromise credentials from public sources and compromised systems, and use compromised cloud identities for persistence and data exfiltration. ARTEX agents can also perform brute-force password attacks, password spraying, API enumeration and abuse, and database dumping. Agentic tools like ARTEX can leverage compromised credentials and systems at machine speed to move laterally, escalate privileges, and exfiltrate data.

This activity illustrates an ongoing trend of threat actors accelerating all stages of the attack chain with agentic AI penetration testing frameworks, including ARTEX. As these capabilities evolve, defenders must similarly use AI to investigate and respond across large environments.

While threat actors regularly use proxies and virtual private networks (VPNs) to change the source IP address of malicious traffic and bypass static detections, Microsoft is providing indicators of compromise (IOCs) to help defenders detect related activity.

Mitigation and protection guidance

Microsoft’s research into threats involving agentic frameworks informs security detections and investigative context across its products. The capabilities available to customers depend on the source of the activity and the products and protections deployed in their environment.

Several behavioral signals can help organizations determine that they are being targeted by threat actors using agentic AI. Agentic AI frameworks scanning a target send a wide variety of requests in a brief time and retry variations on the same technique or move on to next-stage actions at machine speed. Agentic AI frameworks use existing penetration testing tools. For example, ARTEX by default uses Nmap, curl, wget, Python HTTP clients, Norma SDK WebFetch, and headless Chromium through Playwright, among others. These tools may send network traffic with distinctive characteristics, such as default user agent strings. While blocking network traffic with these characteristics will not stop an attack by an AI agent, which will quickly change them, identifying them can alert defenders to the activity.

Defensive honeypots, decoys, tarpits, and fake wins can pull autonomous AI attacks away from legitimate targets. Honeypots and decoy surfaces such as Microsoft Sentinel Deception give the agent attractive but worthless targets to pursue. Tarpits consume the agent’s time and budget. Fake wins present convincing evidence that the agent’s objective is complete, which can cause it to stop on a false success. In Microsoft’s testing, these controls helped reduce the attack traffic reaching real assets and produced high-confidence, attribution-quality signal.

For additional information on the evolution of threat actors’ use of ARTEX please see Microsoft’s recent blogs: AI-driven, large-scale nation-state campaign using ARTEX enables supply chain compromise and Threat actors use agentic AI tooling to find and abuse exposed secrets.

Microsoft’s continuous research into threat actors leveraging agentic frameworks integrates directly into the following products:

Identity and sign-in activity — Microsoft Entra ID Protection

Microsoft analyzes sign-in activity and other signals to identify potential identity risk. Customers can investigate risk detections and risky sign-ins, and configure Conditional Access policies that use sign-in or user risk to require multifactor authentication or block access when specified conditions are met. Identity and sign-in activity from known threat actor infrastructure, including from agentic frameworks like ARTEX, generate Verified threat actor IP risk detections delivered at high risk. See:

Investigate risk with Microsoft Entra ID Protection

Risk-based user sign-in protection in Microsoft Entra ID

What are risk detections? – Microsoft Entra ID Protection

Endpoint activity — Microsoft Defender for Endpoint

Endpoint alerts help security teams identify and investigate suspicious activity on devices. Indicators of compromise can support detection and, when configured, blocking. Customers can review related alerts in the Microsoft Defender portal. See:

Review alerts in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint

Activity across security domains — Microsoft Defender portal

The portal brings together alerts and incidents from Microsoft security solutions and provides relevant threat intelligence to support investigation, threat hunting, and response. This helps customers assess suspicious activity in the context of their own environment. See:

Investigate alerts in Microsoft Defender XDR

Security Dashboard for AI

Threat actor misuse of AI accelerates risk across enterprise environments by amplifying existing threats such as exploitation of vulnerabilities, phishing, malware threats, and insider activity. To help organizations stay ahead of AI-enabled threat activity, Microsoft has introduced the Security Dashboard for AI. The dashboard provides users with a unified view of AI security posture by aggregating security, identity, and data risk across Microsoft Defender, Microsoft Entra, and Microsoft Purview. See:

Security Dashboard for AI

Microsoft Defender detections

Microsoft Defender customers can refer to the list of applicable detections below. Microsoft Defender coordinates detection, prevention, investigation, and response across endpoints, identities, email, apps to provide integrated protection against attacks like the threat discussed in this blog. These alerts may trigger on unrelated activity. Customers should investigate to determine if the alert is related to the activity outlined in this blog.

Tactic

Microsoft Defender coverage

Execution

Microsoft Defender for Endpoint – Process launched in the background – Suspicious file dropped and launched – Suspicious file or content ingress – Hidden file executed – Suspicious process executed by network service – Suspicious piped command launched – Suspicious process launched by service – Suspicious process launched from a world-writable directory – Suspicious script launched – Suspicious shell execution from PHP application – Suspicious shell command execution

Collection

Microsoft Defender for Endpoint – Enumeration of files with sensitive data – Suspicious file copy operations – Suspicious process collected data from local system

Credential access

Microsoft Defender for Endpoint – Suspicious access of sensitive files

Defense evasion

Microsoft Defender for Endpoint – Executable permission added to file or directory – Obfuscation or deobfuscation activity – Possible time based evasion – Suspicious decoding of encoded content into script – Suspicious file and directory permission modification – Suspicious file or information obfuscation detected – Suspicious path deletion

Discovery

Microsoft Defender for Endpoint – Suspicious port scan activity

Command and control (C2)

Microsoft Defender for Endpoint – Possible reverse shell – Suspicious connection to remote service – Suspicious curl behavior Microsoft Defender for Cloud – Publicly accessible storage containers have been exposed – Azure Resource Manager operation from suspicious IP address

Lateral movement

Microsoft Defender for Endpoint – Remote Desktop session

Persistence

Microsoft Defender for Endpoint – Possible Web Server compromise activity – Suspicious cron job creation

Microsoft Security Copilot

Microsoft Security Copilot is embedded in Microsoft Defender and provides security teams with AI-powered capabilities to summarize incidents, analyze files and scripts, summarize identities, use guided responses, and generate device summaries, hunting queries, and incident reports.

Customers can also deploy AI agents, including the following Microsoft Security Copilot agents, to perform security tasks efficiently:

Threat Intelligence Briefing agent

Phishing Triage agent

Threat Hunting agent

Dynamic Threat Detection agent

Security Copilot is also available as a standalone experience where customers can perform specific security-related tasks, such as incident investigation, user analysis, and vulnerability impact assessment. In addition, Security Copilot offers developer scenarios that allow customers to build, test, publish, and integrate AI agents and plugins to meet unique security needs.

Threat intelligence reports

Microsoft Defender XDR customers can use the following threat analytics reports in the Defender portal (requires license for at least one Defender XDR product) to get the most up-to-date information about the activity and techniques discussed in this blog. These reports provide intelligence, protection information, and recommended actions to prevent, mitigate, or respond to associated threats found in customer environments.

Microsoft Security Copilot customers can also use the Microsoft Security Copilot integration in Microsoft Defender Threat Intelligence, either in the Security Copilot standalone portal or in the embedded experience in the Microsoft Defender portal to get more information about this threat.

Hunting queries

Microsoft Defender XDR

Microsoft Defender XDR customers can run the following advanced hunting query to find related activity in their networks:

Download of new files using curl

Threat actors might use tools such as curl to download additional files, communicate with C2 infrastructure, or exfiltrate data. This query looks for new files being downloaded using curl. curl also has legitimate uses, so files and hosts should be reviewed to identify potentially malicious activity.

articles.full_text:
AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) is introducing account access manager, a flexible new way to manage workforce access to your Amazon Web Services (AWS) accounts. This combines the IAM role flexibility your teams already rely on, delivered through the centralized federation of AWS IAM Identity Center, with user-level visibility built-in.

Account access manager streamlines the assignment of your existing IAM roles from individual AWS accounts to your workforce users and groups in an organization instance of IAM Identity Center, giving you a clear path to centralized access management at scale. You can adopt account access manager on its own or alongside IAM Identity Center permission sets; both draw on the same users and groups you already synchronize from your corporate identity provider. That means you assign your existing IAM roles to those users and groups directly, without duplicating identities or managing per-account federation points.

Why use account access manager?

Enterprises scaling on AWS have long faced a difficult choice in workforce access: the flexibility of IAM roles or the central control of IAM Identity Center. Until now, granting workforce access to AWS accounts generally meant choosing one of two approaches, each with trade-offs to consider. Federating into each account separately with IAM roles gives you the full flexibility of IAM roles—custom trust policies, tags, and paths—but requires you to configure an identity provider and manage role assignments independently in each account, making it harder to assign a group across multiple accounts or maintain a unified view of who has access where. Federating once through IAM Identity Center with permission sets gives you a single federation point with centrally provisioned, uniform access, but permission sets can feel restrictive for teams whose roles vary from account to account, or that have difficulty generalizing their existing roles into uniform sets.

Account access manager removes the trade-offs. It’s built for customers who want the single federation point and identity-propagation benefits of IAM Identity Center together with the flexibility of IAM roles. Because it uses the IAM roles you already own, you keep the tailoring capabilities you rely on today:

Attribute-based access control (ABAC) – Use IAM role tags, or session tags populated from your identity provider as SAML claims, for fine-grained, attribute-driven authorization.

Precise trust policies – Restrict role assumption with network conditions or identity provider (IdP)-asserted claims, such as group membership, department, or cost center, as trust-policy conditions.

Role paths for organization at scale – Use IAM role paths to group roles and simplify administration as your environment grows.

Because roles are managed in the account you provision access to, account access manager scales with your account usage rather than relying on Identity Center specific quotas. Assignments are made to users and groups, reducing administrative overhead, and providing accountability and auditability to the specific user and role being used.

How it works

Access flows through IAM Identity Center and carries the user’s identity through trusted identity propagation. Even when multiple users assume a shared IAM role, each role session contains user context that attributes every action to the individual user. Access is granted and audited against the actual user, so you can see who assumed which role in which account. The result is user-level visibility across your organization, not just at the point of sign-in. You also maintain access to the full set of IAM role capabilities, such as role paths, tagging, naming conventions, and other IAM primitives.

Figure 1: Account access manager connects IAM Identity Center federated workforce users and groups to AWS accounts specific IAM roles

To grant a user access to a specific role in an account using account access manager, an administrator creates an entitlement. The user can then access that account from the new account access manager application portal or from their IAM Identity Center access portal, or retrieve credentials from the command line with aws login.

You can manage account access manager through the AWS Management Console for IAM and programmatically through the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) (aws login and the account-access API namespace), AWS SDKs, AWS CloudFormation, and HashiCorp Terraform and Pulumi, so you can enable it and manage role assignments the same way you manage the rest of your AWS infrastructure. It exposes its own API namespace, account-access, separate from the IAM API, with its own permissions and AWS CloudTrail events.

How to enable account access manager

Here’s how to enable account access manager in your own environment, from prerequisites through your first role assignment.

Prerequisites

An organization instance of IAM Identity Center enabled.

Users or groups in IAM Identity Center that you want to entitle with IAM roles from individual AWS accounts. If users or groups don’t exist already then either:

Connect Identity Center to your external identity provider to automatically provision your corporate identities into Identity Center using SCIM.

Create users and groups in the Identity Center directory.

IAM roles in the individual AWS accounts that you want to assign to users and groups of IAM Identity Center. If the role you need doesn’t exist, create a role using custom trust policies first.

Appropriate permissions to enable account access manager and manage assignments (see the IAM policy examples later in this post).

Both the organization instance of IAM Identity Center and account access manager must be enabled in your organization’s management account.

For CLI access: Install or update to the latest version of the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) v2.36.0 or newer.

Step 1: Enable account access manager

Before enabling account access manager, run the following command from the AWS organization management account to grant account access manager access to your organization:

aws organizations enable-aws-service-access --service-principal account-access.amazonaws.com

Next, use one of the following methods to enable account access manager:

Console:

Sign in to your organization’s management account.

In the AWS Management Console for IAM navigation pane, under Multi-account access, choose account access manager.

The console Region should be set to the primary Region of your IAM Identity Center instance.

If there is no organization instance of IAM Identity Center, you’ll be prompted to enable one before continuing. Otherwise, choose Enable account access manager.

Figure 2: Account access manager enablement from the IAM console

AWS CLI:

Fetch the Amazon Resource Name (ARN) of your IAM Identity Center organization instance, confirm the Region code matches its primary Region, and run:

aws account-access create-application \ --region <Region> \ --identity-source '{ "identityCenter": { "instanceArn": "<IAM Identity Center Instance ARN>" } }'

As an output, the account access manager application ARN will be generated.

After you enable account access manager (through the console or AWS CLI), you will get the account access URL and the account access manager ARN along with other details on the capability.

Account access portal URL is the single sign-on entry point for your workforce. This is where your users will go to access AWS accounts. Its format is - https://[Tenant-ID].account-access.[Region].app.aws , found on the Settings tab of the account access manager console.

Account access manager ARN: the identifier for the application instance created when you enable account access manager. Note this ARN to use in your IAM role’s trust policies so that only your specific account access manager application can assume those roles, providing confused-deputy protection (see Step 3 for details) and pass it as --application-arn when creating entitlements using the AWS CLI so each assignment is tied to the correct application instance.

Figure 3: Account access manager settings after enablement

In the AWS CLI, run the command aws account-access list-applications to get the application ARN and tenant-ID of the enabled account access manager instance ARN.

Step 2: Update firewalls and gateways

If you filter access to specific AWS domains or URL endpoints with a next-generation firewall (NGFW) or Secure Web Gateway (SWG), allowlist the account access portal domains and endpoints in the following list. Account access manager has no IPv4-only endpoints; endpoints are dual-stack.

Account access portal URL – https://[Tenant-ID].account-access.[Region].app.aws

Portal APIs – [Tenant-ID].account-access.[Region].app.aws/api/* and /auth/*

Control plane – account-access.[Region].api.aws

Runtime – account-access-runtime.[Region].api.aws

Console – console.aws.amazon.com/account-access

Step 3: Prepare your IAM roles

Before assigning IAM roles to users and groups, update the role’s trust policy to allow account access manager service to assume it.

Add the following statement to the role’s trust policy (or paste the entire policy that follows if you’re creating a new role). Replace <your-account-id>, <region> (your IAM Identity Center primary Region), and <application-id> (from the Settings page of the console).

Figure 4: Account access manager ARN details

IAM role trust policy:

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "AccountAccessManagerIAMRoleTrustPolicyStatement", "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": { "Service": "account-access.amazonaws.com" }, "Action": [ "sts:AssumeRole", "sts:SetContext", "sts:TagSession" ], "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "aws:SourceAccount": "<your-account-id>", "aws:SourceArn": "arn:aws:account-access:<region>:<your-account-id>:application/<application-id>" } } } ] }

Define the Condition block to enforce confused-deputy protection. It helps ensure that the role can be assumed only by the specific account access manager application instance (defined using the application ARN) created when you enabled the service, and only when the request originates from your AWS account where that instance resides.

Best practice:

Propagate identity attributes with ABAC – The sts:TagSession action listed in the preceding IAM role trust policy allows upstream attributes from your identity provider (group memberships, department, cost center) to flow through as principal tags on the session. Without it, role assumption still succeeds; only session-tag propagation is suppressed. Add it when downstream IAM policies use aws:PrincipalTag/<key> and the tag is populated from your IdP SAML claims; leave it out otherwise.

Automate the trust-policy update – We recommend updating your IAM role-creation workflows to add this trust-policy statement automatically wherever it’s needed, so new roles are assignable from day one. You can use this sample-aam-migration tool as a reference.

Step 4: Assign access to users and groups

Like IAM Identity Center role entitlements, an entitlement in account access manager requires three components: a user or group ID, an account ID, and an IAM role ARN (instead of a permission set ARN). You can create assignments from the Accounts, Users, or Groups tabs in the console, or using the API or AWS CLI. For assignments where the same role needs to be assigned to multiple users, you must create each assignment individually. You can automate it using the account access API, the AWS SDK, or AWS CLI.

Assign from the console:

Choose the Users tab and search by username or display name.

Select the user, then choose Assign new access.

Figure 5: Assign new access in account access manager

On the Assign account access page, enter the workforce user or group, account ID, and IAM role name, then choose Assign access.

Assign a user using AWS CLI:

aws account-access create-entitlement \ --region <Region> \ --application-arn "<Account_access_manager_ARN>" \ --entitlement '{ "principalRole": { "principal": { "identityCenter": { "userId": "<Identity_Center_User_ID>" } }, "roleArn": "arn:aws:iam::<ACCOUNT_ID>:role/<ROLE_NAME>" } }'

To assign a group, replace the userId block with "groupId": "<IDC_GROUP_ID>". To remove access, use aws account-access delete-entitlement with the entitlement ID.

Note:

The console can search users, groups, and accounts, but it can’t detect IAM roles because they can come from different AWS accounts in your organization; you must know the role name beforehand.

Only IAM roles whose trust policy grants account access manager as an allowed service principal are eligible for assignment.

IAM role sessions assigned by account access manager use the maximum session duration configured on the underlying IAM role in each AWS account, up to 12 hours.

Step 5: How workforce users can sign in

Workforce users can federate to AWS accounts using IAM roles assigned through account access manager in any of the following ways:

Directly through the account access portal URL – Navigate to the portal URL (for example, https://aa-xxxxxxxxx.account-access.us-east-2.app.aws, or a vanity URL) and sign in.

Through the AWS access portal – Go to the Applications tab, select the Account Access application, and you’ll be redirected to the account access portal, where your assigned accounts and their respective roles are listed.

Tip: We recommend that users bookmark both the account access portal and the AWS access portal for faster navigation. In addition, if you use a supported IdP, such as Okta, Microsoft Entra ID, or Ping Identity, you can add the account access portal as a bookmark app in the IdP’s dashboard, giving users authenticated, single-click access to the portal directly from the tools they already sign in to each day.

Access through a web browser

Use the following steps to use account access manager through a web browser.

Navigate to the account access portal URL and sign in with your credentials.

On the portal, find the AWS account you need. Search by account name or ID to filter the list of accounts you’re assigned to.

Expand the account to see the roles you can assume.

Select a role (for example, Developer). A new tab opens, signed into that account with the selected role.

Access through the AWS CLI

Account access manager works with the aws login command. To get started:

Install the latest AWS CLI (v2.36.0 or newer).

Sign in through your default browser – Sign in to your account access portal and into the target AWS account using one of your assigned roles.

On the AWS CLI, run:

aws login

Set a default Region if prompted – If you haven’t set one, the AWS CLI will prompt you for a Region (for example, us-east-2).

Select your session – The AWS CLI opens a browser page; select the tile for the session you initiated.

Confirm and return to the CLI – The page confirms that your credentials were shared successfully. Close the tab and keep working in the AWS CLI for the duration of your session.

The temporary credentials are automatically rotated by the AWS CLI, AWS Tools for PowerShell, and AWS SDKs, and remain valid for the default session duration of an IAM role. After the session expires, you’re prompted to sign in again on the browser.

Note: IAM Identity Center–specific commands, such as aws sso configure, don’t work with account access manager assignments; use aws login instead. If you want to continue to use aws sso login, refer to AWS CLI Integration for IAM Account access manager.

Create shortcut links to specific console destinations

The portal also lets you create a shortcut link that opens a specific console destination for a given account and role. Shortcut links work only with accounts and roles already assigned to the user—they can’t grant new access—and URL parameters must be URL-encoded. Because shortcut links are Regional and expose the account ID and role name in plain text, review your organization’s sharing policies before experimenting with them.

Customer managed key considerations

If your IAM Identity Center instance is encrypted with an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) customer managed key, which is required when you replicate IAM Identity Center to additional Regions, check the key policy before you enable account access manager. We recommend implementing the current baseline KMS key policy to ensure account access manager can read user, group, and instance data from IAM Identity Center.

Best practices summary

Enable in the right place – Enable account access manager in your organization’s management account and in the same Region as your IAM Identity Center instance and confirm your organization instance is in place before you begin.

Automate trust-policy updates – Build the account access manager trust-policy statement into your role-creation pipelines so every new role is assignable from day one, with no manual intervention.

Add sts:TagSession only when you need it – Include it only where downstream policies consume principal tags; otherwise leave it off to keep sessions lean and least-privilege.

Assign roles to groups, not individual users – Granting access at the group level reduces administrative overhead and strengthens the auditability of user-level access.

Scope administrator permissions tightly – Separate managing the feature from managing assignments, and enable delegating administration to keep day-to-day operations out of the management account.

Allowlist the portal domains before rollout – Add the account access portal domains and endpoints to your next-generation firewall or Secure Web Gateway ahead of launch to avoid access disruptions.

Prepare your workforce users – Have users bookmark both the account access portal and the AWS access portal and communicate the aws login flow clearly to your developers.

Account access manager launch partners

Account access manager launches with a broad ecosystem of AWS identity and access-governance partners who have integrated the service into their existing solutions, making it available to our joint customers from day one. Leading identity providers Okta, PingIdentity and Cisco Duo extend account access manager so customers can manage human workforce access to AWS accounts directly from the identity platforms they already use. Alongside them, access-governance and privileged-access partners Apono, BeyondTrust, Britive, Sonrai Security, C1.ai and Lumos added capabilities to govern, provision, and audit that access through the tooling our customers already rely on.

Account access manager also integrates with leading infrastructure-as-code (IaC) partners, so teams can define and manage access assignments declaratively alongside the rest of their AWS infrastructure. Pulumi enables customers to codify account access manager role assignments as part of their existing provisioning workflows, bringing repeatable, version-controlled automation to workforce access at scale.

Conclusion

Account access manager combines the flexibility of the IAM roles your teams already own with the single, centralized federation point of IAM Identity Center, adding user-level visibility into what users or roles have done across your organization. You assign existing IAM roles to users and groups centrally, scale with your account usage rather than a fixed quota, and give developers a fast, secure command-line experience with aws login. It’s available at no additional cost, enabled by default in Commercial Regions (excluding opt-in Commercial Regions, GovCloud (US), China, and other non-commercial Regions).

To see account access manager in action, watch the enablement video, which walks through enabling the service, preparing your IAM roles, and assigning access to your workforce end to end. You can also extend account access manager through our launch partners; leading identity, access-governance, and IaC providers who have integrated the service into their platforms, so you can govern, provision, and automate workforce access to AWS using the tooling you already rely on. Review the preceding partner integrations to find the ones that fit your environment.

To learn more and get started, visit the AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide. We encourage you to enable account access manager in a test organization, assign your first entitlement, and explore how centralized, user-attributed access can simplify your AWS environment.

Frontier AI is enabling threat actors to rapidly learn an environment, identify weaknesses, and chain them into viable paths to critical systems. These capabilities allow adversaries to move faster while exploiting vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, and other gaps to achieve their goals.

Traditional exposure management helps organizations identify and prioritize weaknesses largely as individual risks, and periodic red team engagements only provide deeper validation at a point in time. Neither approach alone can continuously validate defenses at the speed and scale of AI-enabled adversaries. Organizations must understand not only where they are exposed, but what adversaries could achieve and whether corrective actions can strengthen their defenses.

To fight AI-enabled adversaries with AI, CrowdStrike is introducing Agentic Adversary Emulation, a new AI-powered red teaming capability powered by CrowdStrike® SafeMind. It’s now in early access.

Agentic Adversary Emulation combines specialized AI models and offensive harnesses with real-world adversary intelligence and deep knowledge of customer environments. Operating within controlled, customer-approved boundaries in production environments, it uncovers exploitable attack paths, generates prioritized remediation recommendations and compensating controls, and validates whether corrective actions have strengthened defenses.

Attack Path Discovery to Validated Defense

Reveal Potential Attack Paths

Instead of simply identifying vulnerabilities, Agentic Adversary Emulation shows how attackers could exploit and chain weaknesses across systems and identities to compromise critical assets, and where defenses can stop them. This helps security teams understand what attackers could accomplish in their environment.

Turn Findings into Defensive Action

Agentic Adversary Emulation translates these exploitable attack paths into prioritized remediation actions and compensating controls that security teams can review and deploy through the CrowdStrike Falcon® platform. These may include applying patches, changing configurations, updating security policies, and creating new detections. By connecting demonstrated attack paths to corrective actions, this helps organizations focus on the weaknesses attackers can exploit and take targeted action to disrupt their progress.

Verify that Fixes Work

After corrective actions are implemented, Agentic Adversary Emulation repeats the attack simulation to verify whether those changes successfully disrupt previously identified attack paths. This helps organizations determine whether their fixes work and whether security controls can prevent adversaries from advancing toward critical assets. By connecting attack path discovery, remediation, and validation, Agentic Adversary Emulation creates a closed loop across offense and defense: attack, defend, and validate.
