When individual signals are brought together, a clear picture forms. With Dynamic Risk Scoring (Q4), agent risk feeds into the same 0 to 100 risk score that Falcon Next-Gen SIEM already builds for the agent's owner and host. When an agent, its user, and its device all climb the risk list together, the coordination behind otherwise routine activity is harder to miss.

This foundation extends to the place many of these attacks begin: the AI tooling agents depend on. AI Ecosystem Detections (Q4) add detection logic for attacks on AI services, including LLM API abuse, stolen API keys, and the compromise of coding assistants, MCP servers, and agent frameworks. When the threat starts in a trusted tool rather than the agent itself, the Falcon platform is watching there too.

Because the context around an agent doesn't always live inside the Falcon platform, Federated Search Expansion lets teams search related data where it already lives, without re-ingestion. New connectors for GovCloud, Dynatrace, Databricks, and Snowflake are now generally available, with Splunk, Elastic, and Cribl Lake connectors following in Q4.

Act on Tough Questions

Once a risky agent surfaces, every analyst faces the same question: Did an agent’s owner do this, or did their agent do it without them knowing?

This is the work Multi-Agent Triage and Investigation (GA, announced at Fal.Con US 2026) was built for. SOC agents investigate detections end to end, with specialist agents working the case together on shared context across endpoint, identity, and the agent's activity.

Investigation coverage already spans the full range of Falcon platform and third-party sources. In Q4, triage coverage extends to CrowdStrike Falcon® Guardian, CrowdStrike Falcon® Cloud Security, CrowdStrike Falcon® Shield, CrowdStrike Falcon® Data Security, and custom detections, including abnormal agent behavior flagged by Falcon Next-Gen SIEM. When an agent is flagged, it routes straight into an agentic investigation where the agent, its owner, and its host are already connected.

This shared context is what answers the tough question. Investigating agents can trace a session back to what the person asked for and separate it from what the agent did on its own. When the person's request was routine and everything that followed traces to instructions they never wrote, the verdict becomes clear: The insider was the agent, not the employee.

But a verdict doesn't stop a compromised agent that's still running. The Unified Agentic SOAR Experience (GA, announced at Fal.Con US 2026) is where response happens. Teams build, run, and govern all automation in the SOC, from AI agents to workflows to custom apps, in plain language. They set the mission and define triggers, data, rules, and actions to decide what runs autonomously and what requires approval. A single response decision can coordinate everything that needs to follow in parallel: stopping the agent, cutting off its access, keeping it from coming back, and documenting what happened. It's open by design and connects to any agent, model, or tool through API or MCP, so teams can govern automation across the security stack with visibility into what it's costing and what needs attention.

See it in action:

Autonomy That Earns Its Trust

As SOCs hand more of the work to agents, the controls that keep agents accountable matter as much as the speed they deliver.

CrowdStrike builds governance into every layer of the agentic SOC. It starts by watching the SOC's agents. Policy-Drift Agent Guardrails, powered by Falcon Guardian (Beta, Q4), screen every CrowdStrike Charlotte AI™ and AgentWorks interaction for policy drift, unauthorized tool calls, and out-of-bounds data access to catch the moment an agent steps outside its intended scope.

articles.title: Introducing Sysdig AI Defense: See, stop, and prove what agents do
articles.context: Same sensor codebase, same Falco rules for detections, same threat research
articles.full_text:
AI has moved from assisting to acting. Agents now read files, run commands and reach your cloud with a real person’s access. Most of the time, the only record of what they did is the one the agent wrote itself. “A First Look: Under the Hood of AI Agents” shows where one software company's agents logged one tool call for every seven processes the kernel actually watched them run. And it isn’t only engineers. Someone in finance can wire up a coding agent on a Tuesday afternoon. Every agent, model and seat they add becomes a line item most companies can’t trace to a team or a task.

Find every agent, decide what it can do, keep the record

Sysdig AI Defense is runtime security and governance for every AI agent your teams run, from the laptop where an agent starts its work to the cloud where its actions land.

It starts by showing you what’s there. It finds the agents, MCP servers, skills and plugins your people use, including the ones nobody approved, and ties each one to the account and the person behind it.

Then you decide what agents are allowed to do. Most of the time, nothing changes. Everything your policies don’t name runs as normal, so developers keep working. For the actions you care about, you pick the response. Confirm pauses the call and asks the developer to approve it first. Block refuses it outright. A kill process ends the work the moment the process starts.

Whatever happens, there’s a record. Every action Sysdig AI Defense sees lands in your Sysdig tenant, off the device, where the agent can’t change it. Security can prove what happened, and leaders can see which teams use which models for which work.

Under the hood, it’s the same runtime engine Sysdig built to protect cloud workloads. Same sensor codebase, same Falco rules for detections, same threat research. What’s new is where it looks. It now follows AI agents wherever they work.

By default, Sysdig AI Defense doesn't collect the prompts your people type or the agent's replies. File edits and tool results are removed before they leave the machine. Your data stays in your Sysdig tenant, in the region you choose.

See every agent and MCP server your teams run, then decide what they can use

The questions security leaders ask us most are simple: what agents are running, which ones has nobody approved, and who owns them? Most can't answer these questions yet. In a 2026 IBM study, 77% of organizations surveyed said AI adoption is already outpacing their governance, and two-thirds of the CIOs and CTOs said they are held accountable for AI systems they do not fully control. Sysdig AI Defense answers from what is actually running, across tools like Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and GitHub Copilot, and it follows agents across the whole AI fabric: employee workstations, production Linux and Kubernetes, and the managed agent platforms you don’t own.

Most security teams are likely running more agents than they know about. One software company with about 300 machines found that out in its first month on Sysdig AI Defense. Nothing was blocked, because every policy ran in Alert for the whole month. The full findings are in our “A First Look: Under the Hood of AI Agents”. Half the agents Sysdig AI Defense found on those machines were instances the security team didn’t know about. Employees had signed up with personal email addresses on company devices, outside single sign-on, and every device had at least one agent harness installed and in active use.

Shadow AI isn’t only unapproved agents, either. Early adopters reported finding Ollama, llama.cpp and LM Studio running on people’s machines, a Qwen coding model served locally, and models downloaded straight to laptops. None of that crosses your AI gateway, so the gateway never sees it. The kernel does. It sees each one install, start and pull a model, and ties it to the person behind it.

Once you can see it, you can decide what’s allowed. New AI tools show up in the inventory as they appear on devices. If you don’t want agents using an MCP server, or one of its tools, deny it and set the policy to Block. The agent’s call is refused before it runs, and the agent sees your reason. If there’s a service agents should never send data to, name it in a policy, and kill process ends the upload as the process starts.

‍

Let agents work, and stop only the action that goes too far

An allowlist makes it easy to stop what you already know you don't want. The action itself is harder to judge, because it happens in the middle of a job, often in a fraction of a second. Even the labs that build these models have watched their own agents cross a line. Both OpenAI and Anthropic have disclosed cases where agents working through test tasks reached real systems that belonged to someone else. So the check has to happen at the moment the agent acts. Block and Confirm policies step in on the agent’s tool call before it runs. Kill process catches any process the moment it starts, no matter which agent launched it. You choose which response each policy gets.

Take a file of customer records. Opening one is ordinary work for an agent, and most of the time it is fine. What matters is where the data goes next, and what the agent gave itself permission to do along the way. A read that stays on the machine passes without a second look. The same read, followed by an upload to a public file-sharing host by an agent that just widened its own permissions, is an incident.

When an agent is told no, it tries another route, like a shell command or a script it writes itself. A hook sees the command but is blind to the script. AI Defense sees both. It sees the command with its destination parsed out, and the script as it starts.

You don’t have to write policy from scratch. Start from Sysdig’s managed policies for the risks agents bring, such as MCP servers and tools, secrets and data, and destructive commands. Each one is written as Falco rules you can read. You also don’t have to turn on blocking on day one. Every Sysdig policy starts in Alert, which means it raises what it sees and stops nothing. Watch what it catches on your own fleet. Then choose Block, Confirm or Kill process for the actions that matter. For actions you want a human on, Confirm sends the call to the agent’s own permission prompt, so the developer approves or refuses it right where they’re already working. Security decides which actions need that second look. Everything else runs as normal.

Not every risk fits a rule written in advance. Agents pick up new skills all the time. That’s why Sysdig’s threat research rules also look for agent behavior that resembles an attack, like credential dumping, persistence, tunnels and remote access.

Here’s what that looks like in our demo environment. A revenue operations agent, running with approvals turned off, tries to send a customer export to a public file host. A Kill process policy ends the upload as it starts, and the agent tells the person why.

When security wants to see how it got there, session replay steps through the session’s tool calls in order. The detections and kills show up in the Events rows beside it, each naming the rule and policy that fired.

See which model tier each team uses, for which task

Because every agent is tied to a person, so is every model it uses. Each session carries the model it ran on and the person and team behind it, whether or not the traffic goes through an AI gateway.

That matters for AI spend. In the same findings, four in ten employees ran Opus-class models only. Sysdig AI Defense rates each person’s model tier against how demanding their work was, by team. It flags light work running on the most expensive models, so leaders can change the habit before the invoice shows up. It also flags heavy work on the cheapest models, where someone may be stuck with a model too light for the job. Managers can move them to a better fit and help them get more done.

Answer an audit without pulling developers off their work

When an auditor asks what an agent did and who was behind it, most teams have one place to look, which is the agent’s own log. That log can miss a lot.

The kernel is the part of the operating system every action passes through, which makes it a good place to check. “A First Look: Under the Hood of AI Agents” found that the agent’s own log had no entry for 82% of the credential-file reads the kernel recorded, and no entry for 95% of the reads the agent binary made itself. Across that month, the kernel recorded 2.6 million processes against 374,000 tool calls in the agents’ own logs. The agent’s log is useful context, but it leaves out too much to carry an audit on its own.

Sysdig AI Defense keeps its own record from the kernel, off the device, where the agent can't change it. Remove Sysdig AI Defense’s own hook and it puts it back within the hour, and the kernel keeps recording in between. Each event carries the agent, the account, the model and the session. Each detection names the rule and policy behind it. With Sysdig AI Defense, the evidence is already on file when an audit asks about AI, and nobody has to pull a developer off their work to rebuild it. Teams can also forward these records to their SIEM, where they sit with the rest of their security evidence.

Accountability for agents starts at runtime

Boards are asking what agents are doing, and regulators are starting to ask too. Hatem Naguib, Sysdig's CEO, has boiled it down to three questions every executive should be able to answer:

How do we know our AI isn't going rogue?

What AI are we using, and who is accountable for it?

What can we prove?

None of these can be answered from the agent's own log alone.

Sysdig AI Defense brings to agents the same prevention, detection, and response Sysdig delivers across the cloud, rooted in Falco, the open source runtime security project Sysdig created in 2016 and that the CNCF graduated in 2024. Falco has passed 200 million downloads and is used by more than 60% of the Fortune 500.

Agents will keep getting faster, and their actions will keep reaching deeper into the cloud. The companies that scale them with confidence will be the ones that put the controls in first: every agent known, owned, and tied to an identity; the risky actions stopped as they happen; and a record that holds up afterwards.

See it on your own fleet. Start a free trial and find out what your agents are really doing. Available for macOS and Windows. Sysdig AI Defense runs beside your EDR and can be deployed through your MDM. For the full picture, we recommend rolling it out to at least ten machines.

Most managed service providers (MSPs) have one place where everything about a client lives: their devices, passwords, network details, and the steps for onboarding a new user. For many MSPs, that place is Hudu.

Now your Huntress data can live there too. Hudu has built a Huntress integration that brings your Huntress organizations, agents, memberships, and identities into Hudu and matches them to the client records you already have. It's available now in beta.

Huntress data displayed in Hudu via the Huntress <> Hudu integration

This post covers what Hudu is, what the integration does, how to set it up, and how Hudu built it on the Huntress API.

What Is Hudu?

Hudu is an IT documentation platform for MSPs and internal IT teams. It keeps documentation, passwords, assets, and network details in one structured, searchable place, and more than 6,000 teams use it.

Hudu puts it this way: your PSA manages your work, your RMM manages your devices, and Hudu manages your knowledge. That means the context, credentials, and procedures behind everything those tools touch.

Hudu Dashboard when a user first logs in.

Every client in Hudu is documented with the same structure. That way, any technician can pick up any client without digging through old notes or relying on someone's memory. Hudu also connects with the PSAs, RMMs, and other tools MSPs already use, so that documentation stays accurate. Now Huntress is one of those tools.

How the Integration Works

Once it's set up, Huntress becomes part of each client's documentation in Hudu. A technician can open a client and see the Huntress side of that environment next to everything else:

Which devices have the Huntress agent

Who has access to the client's Huntress organization

Which identities Huntress is protecting

That cuts down on tab-switching during the workday. Say a technician is onboarding a new employee or troubleshooting a laptop. They can confirm Huntress coverage from the same page where they're already working, without logging in to a separate portal to look it up.

The integration also fits the way you've already set up Hudu. Huntress organizations are matched to your existing Hudu companies, so you don't end up with duplicate clients. With Hudu's connected fields, you can map Huntress data to the fields you already use, so it shows up where your team expects it.

Huntress organizations with existing Hudu companies during integration setup.

Setting It Up

Setup takes a few steps:

Create a User API Key in Huntress.

Add your Huntress API credentials to the Huntress integration in Hudu.

Match your Huntress organizations to your Hudu companies.

Map Huntress data to the right asset types and fields in Hudu.

To create your API key, follow our Generating API Keys guide.

How Hudu Built It on the Huntress API

This is the part our Platform team is most excited about. Hudu built this integration themselves on the Huntress API, the same API available to every Huntress partner.

Over the past year, the Huntress API has grown from six read-only endpoints into a full integration and automation platform, along with Webhooks and an MCP server. That means software vendors like Hudu can bring Huntress into their products on their own schedule, without waiting on us.

Huntress API Documentation portal where developers can find the info they need to build custom integrations.

For this integration, Hudu pulls data from the Huntress API's organization, agent, membership, and identity data. Combined with what Hudu already knows about each client, that gives technicians a fuller picture in one place.

"Our customers rely on Hudu to be the single source of truth for every client they support, and Huntress is a big part of how a lot of them keep those clients secure. The Huntress API gave us everything we needed to bring that security context right onto the client page, so technicians can see what's protected without leaving their documentation."

Jordan Hart

Director of Product, Hudu

Ready to Get Started?

Hudu built this integration because MSPs want their security data and their documentation in the same place. The Huntress API made that possible. So where would you like to start?

One Kill Switch with Comprehensive Enforcement Points

Coming soon, CrowdStrike will extend AI Kill Switch beyond gateway enforcement to deliver coordinated agent containment across the Falcon platform.

AI agents operate across endpoints, cloud environments, SaaS applications, browsers, and enterprise identities, often spanning multiple environments in a single chain of activity. When an agent goes rogue, stopping it shouldn't require security teams to investigate and respond separately in every environment.

CrowdStrike's vision is one AI Kill Switch coordinating response across multiple enforcement points. This will bring together the security capabilities of the Falcon platform and its broader ecosystem to contain rogue agents wherever they operate, including:

Endpoint agents: Terminate rogue agents and associated processes directly on affected endpoints and prevent them from restarting.

Cloud agents: Contain or terminate compromised agents operating in cloud environments.

User and agent identities: Leverage CrowdStrike Falcon® Next-Gen Identity Security to revoke agent permissions at runtime and restrict access to enterprise resources.

SaaS agents: Extend containment through CrowdStrike Falcon® Shield to restrict or terminate agent activity within SaaS environments.

Browser sessions: Leverage CrowdStrike Falcon® Seraphic® Enterprise Browser to terminate sessions and disrupt unauthorized activity through web applications.

articles.context: The release arrives nearly a year after developers first requested the feature, bringing Composer into line with package managers that have already adopted minimum release age...
articles.full_text:
Composer 2.11 has introduced dependency cooldowns, giving PHP developers a native way to delay newly published package versions before they become eligible for installation. The release arrives nearly a year after developers first requested the feature, bringing Composer into line with package managers that have already adopted minimum release age policies to reduce exposure to supply chain attacks.

The new config.policy.cooldown setting allows developers to specify a waiting period in hours, days, or weeks. It is disabled by default and applies during dependency resolution, including composer update and composer require. Existing lockfile installations remain unaffected.

The feature also supports organization-wide configuration through Private Packagist, which can enforce cooldowns regardless of the Composer version developers and CI systems are running.

Preventing Cooldown Bypasses #

The original GitHub issue opened in November 2025 and gained urgency following a series of high-profile supply chain compromises. An initial implementation was submitted in December, but the feature missed Composer 2.10 as the maintainers worked through how to enforce cooldowns reliably.

In May, after additional attacks affected Packagist, developers pressed the maintainers for an update. Composer co-founder Nils Adermann explained that the feature was being held up by changes needed to make release metadata trustworthy.

The existing time field in Composer package metadata could be derived from a Git commit date or supplied through composer.json. Both are under the publisher's control, allowing an attacker to backdate a malicious release and bypass a cooldown.

Packagist introduced a new published-time field in June, recording when a version first became available through the registry. Composer 2.11 now uses that timestamp rather than trusting dates supplied by package publishers. Repositories without the required metadata cause dependency resolution to fail unless an explicit fallback is configured.

The cooldown feature is part of a broader security effort by Composer and Packagist. In a May security update, maintainers specifically cited the April compromise of intercom/intercom-php, and the May attack on Laravel Lang among recent incidents affecting the PHP ecosystem. The update outlined several security initiatives, including malware detection, version immutability, and the planned cooldown policy.

Cooldowns Are Now Standard Across Package Ecosystems #

For years, dependency management favored staying on the latest compatible releases. That assumption is changing. With compromised packages appearing on a regular basis, living on the bleeding edge has become considerably less appealing. Cooldowns are increasingly treated as standard supply chain security practice, and some package managers have already made them the default.

Composer is joining a movement already well underway across JavaScript, Ruby, Python, and Rust tooling.

pnpm introduced minimum release ages in September 2025 and made a 24-hour delay the default in version 11. Yarn has also enabled a release-age gate by default, while npm and Bun offer configurable delays. GitHub introduced a three-day default cooldown for Dependabot version updates in July.

In Ruby, Bundler added cooldown support in June, and gem.coop began testing registry-level delays earlier this year. Cargo is next, with minimum publish age support scheduled to become stable in Rust 1.100 on November 12.

Unlike pnpm and Yarn, Composer is leaving the feature opt-in, a decision its maintainers debated during development over concerns about disrupting existing workflows.

Composer also deliberately avoids automatically exempting security fixes. The maintainers rejected that approach because an attacker with publishing access could potentially create an advisory or exploit an existing one to get a malicious release through the cooldown. Developers can use --no-cooldown to install an urgent fix immediately without disabling other security policies. Composer also supports permanent exemptions for specific packages through the cooldown policy's ignore setting.

Security fixes still demand quick updates, especially as AI-assisted vulnerability disclosures accelerate, but for routine dependency updates, cooldowns are becoming best practice. Composer's implementation arrives later than many of its peers, but its adoption adds another major ecosystem to the shift toward giving new dependencies time to be examined before installation.

articles.title: Cloudflare services for private origins is now generally available
articles.context: Today, Cloudflare services for private origins is generally available. Point a proxied DNS record at a private IP, and Cloudflare reaches the origin over your existing Cloudflare One connection<
articles.full_text:
Today, Cloudflare services for private origins is generally available. Point a proxied DNS record at a private IP, and Cloudflare reaches the origin over your existing Cloudflare One connection. Your origin stays private, while web application firewall (WAF), caching, bot management, and Workers work just as they do for public origins.

In June, we launched this capability in closed beta to address a problem we kept hearing from customers: Their internal APIs, AI agent backends, MCP servers, and operational tools weren’t built to face the Internet, but those services still need to accept requests from partners, customers, or agents over the Internet. Before the beta, putting Cloudflare in front of these services meant exposing a public IP, opening a firewall port, or running cloudflared alongside the origin.

Those requirements often left private applications without the same protections and controls they used for public applications, including WAF, bot management, rate limiting, caching, traffic acceleration, rewrites, and Workers.

What is generally available today

During the closed beta, eligible customers requested access through their account team. Today, we’re opening access beyond that beta group.

Point a proxied A or AAAA record at a private IP, and Cloudflare’s application services work as they do for public origins:

WAF and managed rules

Bot management

Rate limiting

Caching

Transform and rewrite rules

Workers

Some limitations remain. Argo Smart Routing and Dedicated CDN Egress IPs aren’t supported, and origin health checks require Load Balancing. See the developer documentation for the full list of current limitations.

Your origin keeps its private IP, with no inbound firewall exception required. With Cloudflare WAN, no connector software on the origin is required. With Cloudflare Mesh, a connector runs within your private network and can serve multiple origins.

How it works

Create a proxied A or AAAA record pointing to your origin. For supported private IP ranges, use private network routing is enabled automatically. If your origin uses a public IP that’s reachable only through your private network, you can enable the setting manually.

The rest of the request flow stays the same: TLS termination, WAF, rules, and caching continue to run on Cloudflare’s network.

The setting turns on automatically for RFC 1918 private IPv4 addresses, RFC 6598 CGNAT addresses (100.64.0.0/10), and RFC 4193 unique local IPv6 addresses (fc00::/7). It can’t be turned off for these ranges; attempts to disable it through the API return an error.

What the API looks like

For customers automating deployments through the API, private routing is simply an additional attribute on a standard DNS record.

POST /zones/{zone_id}/dns_records { "type": "A", "name": "app.example.com", "content": "10.0.0.50", "ttl": 300, "proxied": true, "private_routing": true }

Behind the scenes, Cloudflare's proxy platform determines where to send traffic for app.example.com by querying Cloudflare's Origin API. The response includes metadata indicating that the destination should be reached through a private network path:

{ "zone_name": "example.com", "ipv4_addresses": ["10.0.0.50"], "private_routing": true }

The private_routing flag is the key signal. When our proxy sees it, instead of attempting to connect directly to the private IP address over the public Internet, it hands the request to our private networking layer, which then routes the connection across the customer's existing private network connectivity, whether that's IPsec, GRE, Cloudflare Tunnel, CNI, or Cloudflare Mesh.

The beta post covers the routing layer in more detail.

Get started

Before you begin, you’ll need:

The Private Origins entitlement on your account. Ask your account team to turn it on.

Cloudflare One connectivity using IPsec, GRE, CNI, Cloudflare Tunnel, or Cloudflare Mesh.

Unified Routing enabled on your account, unless you connect over Cloudflare Tunnel (Tunnel doesn't need it). New and existing accounts can upgrade through their account team.

If you connect over Cloudflare WAN or Cloudflare Mesh, configure a return route for Cloudflare’s source ranges: 100.64.0.0/12 for IPv4 and 2606:4700:cf1:5000::/64 for IPv6. Then, create a proxied A or AAAA record for the private IP and confirm that Use private network routing is enabled. Your existing WAF, cache, and bot management configuration applies to that hostname without further changes.

Then, create a proxied A or AAAA record for the private IP and confirm that Use private network routing is enabled. Your existing WAF, cache, and bot management configuration applies to that hostname without further changes.

One note from the beta: if requests time out and nothing arrives at the origin, check the return route first. A missing route for Cloudflare’s source range was the most common setup failure we saw.

Once enabled, follow our developer documentation, which walks through the full setup.

What comes next

Today’s release covers public traffic reaching private origins. Next, we’re working on private-to-private traffic: users, services, and AI agents on private networks reaching applications on other private networks through Cloudflare’s application services.

Engineering work is underway, and we’re targeting a closed beta in early 2027. If you’d like to participate, talk to your account team.

The goal is to give private applications the same protections and controls as public applications. An employee opening wiki.company.internal, for example, could benefit from WAF, rate limiting, and bot management. Service-to-service traffic between clouds and data centers could use those controls too, even when neither side touches the public Internet.

For now, today’s release brings the WAF, caching, bot management, and Workers you use for public applications to private origins over connectivity you already operate.

Questions or feedback? Join the conversation in our community forums or reach out to your account team.

articles.title: Introducing the Microsoft Copilot harness: Unlocking the potential of truly multi-model agentic work
articles.context: If you want to compete, you need to be multi-model. And if you want to take advantage of everything that different AI models have to offer, you need a great harness. articles.full_text:
If you want to compete, you need to be multi-model. And if you want to take advantage of everything that different AI models have to offer, you need a great harness. But building one that works seamlessly across multiple models and surfaces is incredibly hard. You need to solve for performance, quality, and cost. And then you have to maintain it, which is even harder.

Luckily, the GitHub engineering team built a best-in-class, truly multi-model harness, which we’ve adopted company-wide. The Microsoft Copilot harness powers Copilot Code, Copilot Studio, the GitHub Copilot app, the CLI, VS Code, and more. And today, we’re making that harness available through Microsoft Foundry. That gives developers and enterprise customers a fully managed way to build agents that reason, use tools, and complete complex, long-running tasks. You get the right model for the job without switching the harness or the rest of your tech stack. That frees up your time, energy, and resources to focus on your bottom line.

What’s a harness, and why is it hard?

If the model supplies the intelligence, the harness is everything around the model. It’s the orchestration layer that gives an agent the right instructions, context, execution environment, and controls to accomplish meaningful work. And a harness worth its salt has support for open standards like MCP and agent skills, as well as agent plugins.

This is a fast-moving space. A frontier model today might fall behind tomorrow. And building your own harness or model router to keep up can be painful and slow. Now, you can build on the same harness Microsoft and GitHub ship in our own products, and you don’t have to maintain it.

We invest in science and engineering work to continually improve and evolve the harness and ensure high-quality, efficient, and low-cost performance across a range of models and workloads. The benefits compound for us and our customers who use the harness to build and run their own agents. Improve the harness, and every surface it touches benefits.

Born in GitHub, battle-tested at enterprise scale

The Copilot harness was built by the same GitHub engineers behind new technologies like our multi-model orchestration. And those technologies are only possible because we built our own harness. Designed to be fast, token-efficient, and predictable, it was our original, high-quality harness. And it had the highest satisfaction among our most demanding audience: developers. That’s why we’re standardizing all of our Copilot experiences on the strongest foundation possible.

The harness is built to perform across model families, with 20+ frontier models plus bring your own key, so you can use the right model for the right job. Instead of doing the work to keep up with and eval new models, lean on us to intelligently route work to the right model or models based on the task.

Our harness is flexible and configurable to any type of app, agent, or service. We recently ported the harness runtime to Rust, which has resulted in industry-leading performance and reductions in both session overhead and time-to-first token. And because the Copilot harness powers surfaces across Microsoft, it’s battle-tested and proven performant at the scale of millions of users and hundreds of real-world use cases.

A unified harness lets us ship faster, learn faster, and improve Copilot over time. And because the agents you build in Foundry can run on the same harness we’ve adopted across Microsoft, our continuous harness improvements will benefit your agents, too.

Try it yourself

The SDK is available to download, or you can run the harness in the cloud, all managed by Foundry. Our platforms remain open and interoperable, so you can continue to bring in any harness and framework you want, too.

With the Copilot harness, Microsoft runs the agent loop and sandbox, with governance and optimization built in from day one. You bring the instructions, skills, tools, and model choice.

This is an important step towards our vision of a stronger system around the model that preserves choice. It represents the best of GitHub, brought to the Microsoft platform and beyond.

We’ll keep pushing the harness forward, so you can focus on what only you can build.

articles.full_text:
Your workloads reach most destinations by domain name, but a firewall can only act on what it sees in the traffic. For HTTP and HTTPS, AWS Network Firewall domain rules match the name that the client puts in the request, and the client chooses that name. The connections for protocols such as SSH and SSH File Transfer Protocol (SFTP) don’t carry the domain name. The client uses the name only for the DNS lookup and then connects straight to the IP address that DNS returned. As a result, Network Firewall rules for these protocols have used IP addresses, which change over time. For web and non-web traffic alike, Network Firewall had no view of the answers that your DNS resolver returned, because that shared visibility between DNS and the firewall didn’t exist.

On October 21, 2026, we launched Route 53 Resolved IP Validation for AWS Network Firewall, at no additional charge. Amazon Route 53 Resolver now shares the IP addresses that it returns for each domain name with Network Firewall, and Network Firewall checks each new outbound connection against them. With this launch, you can now filter non-web traffic by domain name, and you can prevent Server Name Indication (SNI) manipulation on TLS traffic without needing to enable TLS inspection.

In this post, we explain how the feature works, show how to turn it on in alert mode, and walk through two common use cases. They’re examples; the same check applies to any outbound traffic that you control by domain name.

How it works

Amazon Route 53 Resolver answers DNS queries from resources in your virtual private cloud (VPC) configured to use it, and it’s available by default in every VPC. With this feature, Route 53 Resolver keeps the IP addresses that it returns for each domain name in a resolved IP cache. When a new outbound connection starts, Network Firewall checks the destination address against that cache.

The workload asks Route 53 Resolver at 10.0.0.2 for files.partner.example.com.

DNS Firewall checks the query first. Domain rules can block or alert on it; an empty rule group lets it through.

Route 53 Resolver answers 203.0.113.10 and records the answer in the resolved IP cache.

The SFTP connection to 203.0.113.10 on port 22 reaches the Network Firewall endpoint.

The policy checks the first packet. The address is in the cache, so the connection continues.

The stateful rule passes it, because Route 53 Resolver returned the address for files.partner.example.com.

The connection leaves through the NAT gateway and internet gateway.

The flow log and alert log record the new fields.

The feature has three parts:

An Amazon Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall rule group – It defines the scope. The answers that Route 53 Resolver returns in every VPC associated with this rule group go into the resolved IP cache. The rule group can be empty. Add rules to it and the same rule group also filters the DNS queries themselves, for example, by blocking lookups of known threat domains. Together, DNS Firewall checks the lookup and Network Firewall checks the connection that follows.

The Network Firewall policy setting – On the first packet of each new connection, before your stateful rules run, Network Firewall checks whether Route 53 Resolver returned the destination address for a domain name. If it did, the connection continues to your stateful rules. If it didn’t, Network Firewall applies the action you chose: Alert, Drop, or Reject.

Resolved-domain rules – In your stateful rule groups, these rules match a connection by the domain name that its destination address was resolved for, so they work with every protocol. Use the name that your clients look up.

The following diagram shows this architecture.

Figure 1. How Network Firewall checks the SFTP connection from use case 1 against the answers that Route 53 Resolver returned

The policy setting checks every connection, not only web traffic. A connection to an IP address that no client looked up through Route 53 Resolver, such as a hardcoded address, fails the check. If any of your workloads connect straight to IP addresses, add those addresses to Bypass destination validation IP ranges before you enforce. A stateful pass rule doesn’t exempt them because the policy check runs before your rules. The check is per address: when any client in an associated VPC looks up a name, its addresses pass the check for every client in scope in the same Availability Zone. For details, see Resolved IP validation in AWS Network Firewall in the AWS Network Firewall Developer Guide.

Prerequisites

To follow along, you need:

DNS through Amazon Route 53 Resolver – Network Firewall can check only answers that Route 53 Resolver returned. Queries that reach Route 53 Resolver through Resolver endpoints or Resolver forwarding rules count.

A Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall rule group associated with the VPCs whose DNS answers Network Firewall should check connections against.

The policy setting turned on before you add resolved-domain rules – Rules that use domain filtering (the aws_route_53_resolved_domain keyword) need Route 53 Resolved IP Validation turned on in the same firewall policy. Turn the setting on first, in alert mode, then add the rules.

A supported deployment model – The feature works with distributed deployments, including multiple firewall endpoints, where clients reach a firewall endpoint in their own Availability Zone, and with centralized deployments where the firewall is attached natively to AWS Transit Gateway. If routing sends a client to a firewall endpoint in another Availability Zone, its connections fail the check. To move a centralized deployment to a natively attached firewall, see Why and how to migrate to a Transit Gateway attached AWS Network Firewall.

How to turn it on in alert mode

Start in alert mode because clients cache DNS answers. Network Firewall recognizes only the answers that Route 53 Resolver returns after the DNS Firewall rule group is associated with the VPC and selected in the policy. A client that still uses an answer it cached earlier fails the check until it looks up the name again, usually when its cached record expires. Alert mode lets you see this without blocking anything. Allow about 24 hours in alert mode for clients to refresh their caches.

Create a DNS Firewall rule group (it can be empty) and associate it with the VPCs whose DNS answers Network Firewall should check connections against. For the steps, see Creating a rule group and rules.

Or, to use a DNS Firewall rule group that you already have, make sure it’s associated with those VPCs and only those. An answer returned in any associated VPC is valid for every client that the firewall checks. Which clients are checked is set by source IP ranges in step 6.

In the Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) console, under Network Firewall, choose Firewall policies, then choose the policy that your firewall uses. On the Traffic inspection tab, in the Route 53 Resolved IP validation section, choose Edit and select Enable Route 53 Resolved IP validation.

For Action, choose Alert. For DNS Firewall rule group, choose the rule group from step 1 or 2.

For DNS expiry exception policy, choose what happens to a connection that’s already open when its entry expires from the resolved IP cache. Continue keeps it running, Drop stops it silently, and Reject stops it with a TCP reset. We recommend Continue so that long-running sessions, such as file transfers, aren’t cut off midway. However, choose the option that fits your security requirements.

For source IP ranges, list the clients to check. If you don’t set it, Network Firewall checks clients in the firewall’s VPC and in any additional VPCs attached to the firewall. If your clients are in other VPCs, such as spoke VPCs that send traffic to a firewall attached to a transit gateway, enter their CIDR ranges; otherwise, Network Firewall doesn’t check their connections. Add destinations that you allow by IP address to Bypass destination validation IP ranges. Choose Save.

The following screenshot illustrates these steps.

Figure 2. Route 53 Resolved IP Validation turned on in alert mode

In alert mode, Network Firewall doesn’t block a connection that fails the check, and it doesn’t write an alert of its own. It records the result in your flow logs, in the route53_resolved_ip field of each connection. A value of true means Route 53 Resolver returned the destination address for a domain name. A value of false means it didn’t, so enforcement would block the connection. The same field also appears in alert log records that a rule or the policy’s default action writes for the connection. Pass rules don’t write one unless they have the alert; keyword. The DnsUnresolvedFlows metric in Amazon CloudWatch counts the connections that fail the check, and DnsAzUnavailableFlows counts connections from an Availability Zone that doesn’t support the feature. The following alert log record (trimmed, with example values) was written by a default action that alerts, for a connection to an address that Route 53 Resolver returned:

{ "firewall_name": "egress-firewall", "availability_zone": "us-east-1a", "event": { "event_type": "alert", "src_ip": "10.0.1.10", "dest_ip": "203.0.113.10", "dest_port": 123, "proto": "UDP", "app_proto": "ntp", "route53_resolved_ip": true, "verdict": { "action": "alert" }, "alert": { "action": "allowed", "signature_id": 3, "signature": "aws:alert_established action" } } }

In alert mode, this record is for a TLS connection that presented an allowed domain name but went to an address that Route 53 Resolver didn’t return for it, blocked by the policy’s default action in use case 2:

{ "firewall_name": "egress-firewall", "availability_zone": "us-east-1a", "event": { "event_type": "alert", "src_ip": "10.0.1.10", "dest_ip": "198.51.100.7", "dest_port": 443, "proto": "TCP", "app_proto": "tls", "tls": { "sni": "api.partner.example.com" }, "route53_resolved_ip": false, "verdict": { "action": "drop" }, "alert": { "action": "blocked", "signature": "aws:alert_established_app_layer_to_server action" } } }

Before you switch Action to Drop or Reject, check that connections that fail the check are ones you expect and that destinations you allow by IP address are in the bypass ranges. Reject sends a TCP reset, so a blocked TCP client fails right away instead of waiting for a timeout. After you enforce, blocked connections appear in your flow logs with route53_resolved_ip as false, not in your alert logs. For the metrics and log fields to watch, see Monitoring and troubleshooting resolved IP validation.

Use case 1: Filter non-web traffic by domain name

Before this launch, Network Firewall rules for protocols that carry no domain name, such as SFTP, used IP addresses. Now, you can allow them by domain name. In this example, a workload sends files over SFTP to a partner at files.partner.example.com on TCP port 22, and the partner can change the addresses behind that name at any time. The same approach works for SSH, MySQL, and other non-web protocols. You create it as a standard stateful rule. Follow these steps:

Under Network Firewall, choose Network Firewall rule groups, then choose Create rule group. Choose Stateful rule group and Standard stateful rule, and choose the rule evaluation order that your policy uses.

Choose Add rule. For Protocol, choose TCP. For Destination port, enter 22. Under Domain filtering, enter files.partner.example.com. For Action, choose Pass.

Create the rule group, then add it to your firewall policy.

Figure 3. A pass rule for SFTP on TCP port 22, scoped to the partner’s domain name

If you manage rules as code, the equivalent Suricata rule is shown in the following code. It adds the alert; keyword so that the firewall logs allowed connections. The console rule doesn’t add it.

pass tcp any any -> any 22 (alert; msg:"Allow TCP/22 to files.partner.example.com"; aws_route_53_resolved_domain:"files.partner.example.com"; sid:1;)

When the partner moves its server to a new address, the next DNS answer adds it to the resolved IP cache. There’s no IP list to maintain. The cache keeps earlier answers for longer than their DNS time to live (TTL), so the old address can still pass for a while.

Use case 2: Prevent SNI spoofing without TLS inspection

With SNI spoofing, a client presents an allowed domain name in its TLS request while it connects to a different server. Preventing that has required TLS inspection, which decrypts the traffic. Route 53 Resolved IP Validation prevents it without TLS inspection. In this example, a workload calls a partner API at api.partner.example.com over HTTPS. TLS traffic on port 443 must reach only the addresses that Route 53 Resolver returned for that name. You create a pass rule in a standard stateful rule group, as in use case 1, and the firewall policy’s default action drops everything that no rule passes. Follow these steps:

Under Network Firewall, choose Network Firewall rule groups, and then choose Create rule group. Choose Stateful rule group and Standard stateful rule, then choose Strict order.

Choose Add rule. For Protocol, choose TLS. For Destination port, enter 443. Under Domain filtering, enter api.partner.example.com. For Action, choose Pass.

Create the rule group, then add it to your firewall policy.

In the firewall policy, use strict rule order. For the stateful default actions, choose Application drop established (server-directed only) and Application alert established (server-directed only). The alert action logs what the drop action blocks. For why we recommend these default actions, see Firewall policy configuration in the AWS Security Services Best Practices guide.

Figure 4. A pass rule for TLS on port 443, scoped to the partner’s domain name

If you manage rules as code, the equivalent Suricata rule is:

pass tls any any -> any 443 (aws_route_53_resolved_domain:"api.partner.example.com"; sid:2;)

The pass rule matches the destination address, not the name in the TLS request. TLS traffic on port 443 passes only when Route 53 Resolver returned the destination address for api.partner.example.com. If the partner’s addresses also serve other domain names, such as behind a content delivery network (CDN), those names pass too. To also require the partner’s name in the TLS request, add an exact SNI match to the same rule: tls.sni; content:"api.partner.example.com"; startswith; endswith; nocase;.

Without startswith and endswith, the content match accepts any SNI that contains the name.

A connection that presents the partner’s name but goes to another address doesn’t match the pass rule. If Route 53 Resolver never returned that address, the policy setting’s enforcement action blocks the connection before your rules run. In alert mode, the policy setting lets the connection through to your rules instead, and the stateful default action drops it because the pass rule doesn’t match. Its alert log record shows route53_resolved_ip as false, as in the second example previously. If Route 53 Resolver returned the address for a different domain name, the connection passes the policy check. The stateful default action then drops it because the pass rule doesn’t match, and that record shows route53_resolved_ip as true.

Best practices

We recommend that you follow these best practices:

Keep DNS on Route 53 Resolver – Block outbound UDP and TCP port 53 DNS to other resolvers, including DNS over HTTPS (DoH) and DNS over TLS (DoT), on Network Firewall, so that clients don’t bypass the check. Route 53 Resolved IP Validation alone doesn’t do this. If any client looks up a public resolver’s name, such as dns.google, that resolver’s addresses pass the check.

Keep DNS Firewall rules in those VPCs – Route 53 Resolved IP Validation checks the connections that follow a DNS lookup, not the DNS queries themselves. DNS Firewall blocks lookups of known threat domains with AWS managed domain lists, and its advanced rule groups detect data leaving through DNS queries, such as DNS tunneling.

Start small – Add domain filtering to a few rules at a time, then add more when the results look clean. For domain allow list patterns, see Allow rules and domain allowlisting.

Turn on flow and alert logging and detailed monitoring – Connections that fail the resolved IP check show in your flow logs (route53_resolved_ip: false) and in the DnsUnresolvedFlows metric, not in your alert logs. Pass rules without the alert; keyword don’t write an alert log record.

Pricing and availability

Route 53 Resolved IP Validation is available today in all commercial AWS Regions (Regions other than the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions and the China Regions) where AWS Network Firewall and Amazon Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall are available, at no additional charge. For the list of Regions, see AWS Capabilities by Region. A DNS Firewall rule group with no rules doesn’t incur DNS Firewall charges. Standard DNS Firewall pricing applies after you add rules. See AWS Network Firewall pricing and Amazon Route 53 pricing.

Conclusion

In this post, we showed you how Route 53 Resolved IP Validation works and how to turn it on in alert mode. Network Firewall now checks each connection’s destination against the IP addresses that Amazon Route 53 Resolver returned for the DNS query. Filtering SFTP, SSH, database, and other non-web traffic by domain name and preventing SNI spoofing without TLS inspection are two common examples of what that makes possible. To get started, turn the feature on in alert mode and review the results before you enforce. For the full walkthrough, see Getting started with resolved IP validation.

To learn more, visit the AWS Network Firewall product page and the feature documentation.

articles.title: ISC2 Launches Cyber-AI Workforce Coalition to Address the Future of AI Security Jobs
articles.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
articles.full_text:
After years of tracking the global cybersecurity skills gap through its annual Cybersecurity Workforce Study, ISC2 is taking a more active role in shaping the future of the profession with the launch of its Cyber-AI Workforce Coalition.

Announced on October 20, the new coalition is one of the first major developments introduced by Scott Beale, ISC2’s CEO, who took on the role in December 2025.

Speaking to Infosecurity during the ISC2 Security Congress 2026, in Denver, Colorado, on October 26, Beale said he spent his first six months as CEO listening to the organization’s members.

A key finding from the consultation was that a majority of ISC2 members want the nonprofit to more ambitiously and vocally step into the AI safety and security space.

“We want to be the association that can help prepare the cybersecurity workforce for the many challenges of this AI era,” Beale added.

Mapping the AI Security Workforce and Its Emerging Skills Gap

Beale described the coalition as a “vendor-neutral convener” for global cybersecurity professionals. It aims to include thought leaders like HR managers and CISOs, some of the largest employers of cybersecurity practitioners, standard-setting bodies and even government representatives to discuss how cybersecurity roles are changing because of AI.

“Even as the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) and others are updating standards and frameworks, companies are still facing a lack of resources for how to best advertise and fill these roles. How a bank describes these jobs is still very different from how a hospital would,” Beale said.

Hiring needs at the intersection of AI and cybersecurity remain uncertain, according to Beale. There remain unanswered questions about how AI will affect future demand for cybersecurity professionals, which skills will be most critical for AI security roles, and how experienced practitioners can upskill to meet emerging demands.

“The coalition a way for us to listen directly to these people and help move the sector in a way that can be responsive to their needs,” he said.

Practical Tools to Define and Hire for AI Security Roles

In practice, the coalition will not create new standards or frameworks but will instead focus on delivering toolkits for employers to help them describe new job roles at the intersection of AI and cybersecurity.

These toolkits will include guidance for how employers hire, develop and organize cybersecurity talent, and how practitioners can identify and build the expertise employers need.

These new tools will help answer three main questions:

How are cybersecurity jobs changing?

How are employers writing job descriptions for these new roles?

How are candidates preparing to interview and fill these jobs?

“As you know, ISC2 is working on a new AI security certification, and certainly we think It is going to be part of that answer and will help us define some of these new roles,” he said. “However, by no means do we pretend having the only solution to this problem.”

The coalition will hold its first meeting in November. Beale hopes it can develop its first series of toolkits by the spring of 2027 and have some companies using them in a pilot phase to help them hire AI security professionals.

The tools produced by the coalition are expected to eventually be made available for everyone to use, not just ISC2 members. Beale believes they will also be useful for universities and certification bodies to adapt their curriculums.

articles.title: Introducing the Cloudflare PHP Capture the Flag challenge
articles.context: We shipped client updates and multiple mitigations, updated our web application firewall (WAF) with new rules to block attackers from exploiting the PHP vulnerabilities, and...
articles.full_text:
Last week was one for the Internet security history books. First, eight eMudhra intermediate certificates were compromised, creating the possibility of forged certificates that could be used to impersonate servers. Then came php2shell: serious vulnerabilities in PHP, the runtime behind a large portion of the Web.

Cloudflare worked around the clock as these events unfolded to protect our customers and help protect the Internet. We shipped client updates and multiple mitigations, updated our web application firewall (WAF) with new rules to block attackers from exploiting the PHP vulnerabilities, and introduced a new feature called full transaction detection.

As always in situations like this, these new capabilities were made available on all plans, including Free.

Put our WAF to the test

Protecting systems from vulnerabilities like these is always an ongoing process, not a one-time event. The widespread adoption of AI allows attackers to discover new vectors with unprecedented speed and efficiency, so collecting real-world data to test our assumptions and strengthen defenses is essential.

That’s why today we're launching the Cloudflare PHP Capture the Flag challenge, run through our Bug Bounty program. We've put a deliberately vulnerable PHP installation behind our WAF, and we're inviting security researchers on HackerOne to try to bypass the protections and capture a flag.

How this Capture the Flag (CTF) works

We are keeping this simple. The challenge focuses on CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, the two PHP vulnerabilities behind php2shell. The target runs stock PHP 8.5.11 (with standard PHP extensions), Apache 2 (via mod_php), and an empty index.php inside a Cloudflare Container, with our default WAF protection rules for these vulnerabilities enabled in front of it. Inside the sandbox is a file called /flag.

The sandbox is reset every few minutes, including the flag file.

Your mission, should you choose to accept it: bypass the WAF protections, exploit the PHP sandbox, and recover the contents of /flag. You can use your own research tools. The challenge page has the environment details, scope, and flag verification form.

Challenge requirements

This limited-time challenge is run via Cloudflare's Bug Bounty program on HackerOne. All aspects of this challenge are subject to HackerOne terms and the Cloudflare HackerOne program rules the (“Bounty Terms”). If you find an eligible bypass, you must follow these requirements in order to claim the bounty:

All participants must sign up for a HackerOne account and review and agree to the Bounty Terms before participating in the CTF.

Demonstrate attacker-controlled PHP code or command execution inside the sandbox through an authorized POST request.

Use that remote code execution (RCE) to recover the current contents of /flag, then successfully verify the flag through the CTF user interface (UI). Verify promptly before a reset; retain the successful result for later review.

Submit a private report to Cloudflare on HackerOne. Include PHP CTF in the title and provide:

The endpoint, complete payload, and request sequence, preserving relevant headers, encoding, and body bytes.

Raw request/response captures or a readable proof of concept sufficient to reproduce the full chain.

An explanation of the WAF bypass, executed code or command, and how that execution recovered /flag.

The attempt ID, successful UI verification result, and exploit/verification UTC timestamps. Include the flag privately if needed for verification.

What makes the method or payload materially distinct, and related submissions you know about.

UI verification does not submit a HackerOne report or establish reporting priority. File disclosure without RCE, RCE without successful flag recovery and UI verification, local-only exploits, rediscovery of the known PHP vulnerabilities, and WAF detection differences or partial chains without the full objective are not eligible.

Awards require a materially distinct Firewall (WAF) bypass method, even for the same PHP CVE. Reports using the same Firewall-bypass mechanism are duplicates, regardless of differences in the PHP exploit, payload, RCE technique, or flag-recovery method. New flags, resets, attempt IDs, or cosmetic changes—including equivalent encodings—do not qualify as unique. Equivalent submissions are duplicates even if unfixed; only the first complete, reproducible HackerOne report is considered. Cloudflare makes final duplicate and reward decisions.

We record attempted metadata and request payloads to help analyze reports, so please use test data only. Do not send credentials, personal information, or anything else you would not want included in a research record. Read Cloudflare’s privacy notice before testing.

Testing is authorized only against the challenge hostname's WAF-protected /php/* endpoints (POST method only). Other Cloudflare services, direct access to the underlying infrastructure, the upstream PHP project, and third-party systems are out of scope. No denial of service, high-volume scanning, persistence, social engineering, or attacks on other participants. If you get a 429 or 503, back off.

In the event of any conflict between this blog post and the Bounty Terms, the Bounty Terms shall prevail.

Cloudflare reserves the right to suspend or terminate this challenge at any time. Once the competition is removed from HackerOne, it is officially terminated, so please refer to the Cloudflare HackerOne page for the most up-to-date information on whether this challenge remains open.

Not a substitute for patching

Our WAF protects you, but it is not a replacement for fixing vulnerable software. Response blocking can prevent exposed data from reaching an attacker, but it cannot undo actions already performed at the origin. If you run PHP, follow the latest PHP security advisories and apply the relevant updates.

Last week was a reminder that helping build a better Internet often takes many people—researchers, maintainers, and teams across the industry—doing difficult, urgent work together.

We hope this challenge gives everyone a useful way to join in. Head over to php-rce.cloudflare.app if you want to participate: the flag is there, and we'd like to know if you can get it.

articles.title: Cisco Expands Partner Opportunity with New Cisco 360 Program Updates, High Yield Customer Experience Offerings, and AI-Ready Innovations
articles.context:
Enhancements give every partner a path to move first and fast in the AI era
More RSS Feeds:
articles.full_text:
News summary:

Cisco introduces Ecosystem Deal Registration alongside new incentives and AI-enabled tools for partners to recognize and support our ecosystem at every step of the deal.

General availability of Cisco IQ for partners provides new profitability avenues and growth opportunities.

Expanded Cisco Cloud Control offerings provide partners with new ways to build, secure, and manage AI-ready infrastructure.

VANCOUVER, BC – October 26, 2026 – AI is moving infrastructure to the center of enterprise investment, creating a critical market opportunity to modernize, scale, and secure the networks that power the AI era. To help its partners lead this transformation, today at Cisco Partner Summit, Cisco (NASDAQ: CSCO) unveiled new advancements across its partner program, customer experience offerings and technology portfolio, providing the tools and incentives required to capture this next wave of global connectivity growth.

Expanded incentives within the Cisco 360 Partner Program combined with the general availability of Cisco IQ for Partners address the demand for more agility and intelligence in the current environment. Cisco Cloud Control continues to bring it all together, giving Cisco partners, IT professionals and AI agents a platform where they can work together to connect, protect and run the critical infrastructure for the AI era.

“Our partners are where Cisco meets the customer, and the AI era is asking more of all of us,” said Tim Coogan, SVP, Global Partner Sales, Cisco. "Customers need partners with the agility to move first and fast. By combining the strength of the Cisco 360 Partner Program with Cisco IQ and Cisco Cloud Control, we’re giving every type of partner new ways to deliver that and be rewarded for it, from the advisor who shapes a decision to the partner who delivers and supports it."

Powering an Agile Partner Ecosystem

Advisors, Developers, and Distributors increasingly shape what customers buy as well as how it's delivered, and as the Cisco 360 Partner Program enters its first full year, the program has added dedicated paths for each of them. Additional enhancements span program experience, profitability and enablement for all partner types, empowering true ecosystem agility in the AI era, and rewarding the contributions of every partner.

Ecosystem Deal Registration: A new way for Advisors and Developers to be formally recognized for contributions that lead to transactions, validating partner impact across the customer lifecycle.

New growth paths: Advisor and Developer Partner Value Indexes (PVIs) are now available and a new unified Distributor PVI will be available by Spring of 2027, underscoring Cisco’s commitment to measuring partner contributions based on the unique value their role brings to the customer.

Evolution of Cisco Partner Incentive (CPI) Rates: A continued investment in partner value exchange,increasing ACV growth reward by 50% as well as a 2x increase on Adopt for all use cases, as well as launching new adopt incentives on Cisco IQ.

Additional +2% Cross-Sell Bonus: An incremental +2% on top of the existing cross-sell rebate for Preferred and Portfolio partners expanding customer accounts into net-new Cisco architectures, including Splunk.

Cisco IQ Adopt Incentive: Designed to reward Partner adoption of Cisco IQ to ensure customers are onboarded and integrated with their telemetry.

Additionally, enhanced partner experience resources are now available to help partners differentiate and expand their offerings for customers:

Deal registration visibility in Partner Experience Platform (PXP): Automated, real-time insights to optimize pipeline health and enable partners to identify growth opportunities.

Advanced Trend Analysis and Eligibility Tracking: New PVI APIs enable partners to optimize their business outcomes and proactively manage their performance.

On-demand agentic resource: The One Cisco Content Agent (beta) makes it easy for partner sellers and marketers to quickly access approved Cisco content and customize value propositions for every customer tailored to specific priorities and industry trends, creating relevant co-branded presentations in minutes rather than hours.

New CPI Deal Estimator: Empowers partners to model deal economics and optimize rebate yield across every opportunity.

New OT certification: To reflect the growing convergence of IT, OT, and security, Learn with Cisco is launching a new Cisco OT Security Practitioner certification and releasing Cisco Modeling Labs 2.11 with new hands-on lab capabilities.

Cisco IQ: New Partner Opportunities for Profitable Services

Customers crave the ability to better understand their IT environments, intuitively identify risk, and quickly act before issues impact business outcomes. Partners need that same level of visibility so they can deliver more relevant, higher-value services to customers and propose modernization opportunities. Today, Cisco is announcing the general availability of Cisco IQ for Partners, empowering its global partner ecosystem to drive repeatable, high-margin growth across both managed services and reseller models. With more than 16,000 customers, and with visibility across close to 20 million devices since April 2026, the extension of Cisco IQ to partners provides new opportunities for growth after deal closure:

Deliver differentiated managed services: With Cisco IQ MCP Server and expanded API access, partners can seamlessly integrate intelligence into their own professional services, workflows, and AI agents. This enables partners to instantly query customer estates so they can address short term risks like emerging AI-powered threats, while helping customers plan for infrastructure modernization.

Secure, automated capabilities for Resellers: Through new Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) in Cisco IQ, customers can grant partners direct, secure visibility into their installed base. This transforms resellers into intelligence-led partners who can leverage real-time data and APIs to operate at machine scale—spotting hidden network risks, eliminating manual exports, and proactively driving customer modernization.

Cisco is also introducing new Cisco IQ capabilities for customers and partners:

New AI-Powered Quantum Safe and Software End of Vulnerability Support (EoVS)playbooks to help identify risks beyond routine patching.

Priority Bugs & Software Conformance Assessments to spot outage risks, prioritize remediation, and scope upgrades or hardening services.

Frictionless Cisco Cloud Control integration surfacing real-time risk intelligence, including quantum-readiness status, and enabling one-click action on at-risk, controller-managed devices directly within Cloud Control.

Cisco IQ AI Assistant enhancements based on rich contextual real-time data with troubleshooting now informed by device diagnostics and Cisco Technical Assistance Center (TAC) knowledge. Simplified TAC case management means you can create, close, and escalate a TAC case from within the AI Assistant.

"For too long, partners walked into customer conversations without the same view Cisco had. That changes today,” said Liz Centoni, EVP and Chief Customer Experience Officer, Cisco.

“With Cisco IQ Partner Support Standard, partners get that same intelligence under their own brand, delivered through their own experts. It's their name. Their customer relationship. Their services practice. Cisco IQ is the engine. Partners are the business."

Resilient, Secure, and AI-Ready Infrastructure Innovations

As enterprises scale AI agents across wired and wireless networks, they face mounting risks from downtime, visibility gaps, and identity-based threats. Cisco Cloud Control addresses these challenges by providing a shared, unified operations platform for teams and AI agents to secure and manage critical infrastructure across IT domains. To further enable machine-speed collaboration and automation, we are introducing new AgenticOps capabilities to Cloud Control, including:

Model Foundry:A new platform service in Cisco Cloud Control for putting Cisco’s purpose-built models to work — discovering, evaluating, fine-tuning, and running them on your own data, all in one place. Model Foundry is also the exclusive home of Cisco’s newest model versions and weights before broader release. Controlled Availability begins with Cisco partners.

ThousandEyes intelligence for trusted autonomous operations: Cisco is integrating ThousandEyes natively into Wi-Fi 6E and 7 access points, included with eligible Cisco Networking Essentials and Advantage licenses. With nothing additional to buy, deploy, or configure, always-on ThousandEyes enables automated background testing that is designed to validate application and network performance around the clock even when no users are online and strengthens customer trust in agentic actions.

Agentic integration: Cisco is introducing Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers for its networking platforms, which act as a standardized bridge that allows AI tools to easily access live network data. This removes the need for partners to build and maintain complex custom connections, making it simpler to create automated workflows for tasks like troubleshooting and reporting, while helping IT teams identify and resolve issues faster by linking deep telemetry directly to actionable experience metrics.

“The future of infrastructure operations is agentic, and it requires a platform that combines shared context, purpose-built models, and clear guardrails. Cisco Cloud Control is that platform,” said Jeetu Patel, President and Chief Product Officer, Cisco. “With the new Model Foundry, we’re advancing the state of the art in AgenticOps further. Enabling partners to fine-tune and customize Cisco’s models for their customers’ environments will make them integral to how their customers connect, protect, and run their infrastructure.”

To deliver the hardened physical and digital foundation required to connect, power, and protect mission-critical workloads for the long term, Cisco is introducing new resilient and quantum-safe innovations, including:

Extending quantum readiness across wireless networks: Cisco is launching the industry's first Wi-Fi 7 access point with quantum-resilient capabilities. This is the latest addition to the most comprehensive quantum-resilient networking portfolio, spanning wireless, switching, and routing, enabling partners to deliver quantum-readiness assessments and future-proof customer infrastructure investments well into the next decade. For quantum-safe communications with Post Quantum Cryptography over the air, Cisco provides Qualcomm Technologies-powered access points while the complete client-side solution is supported by an Intel Wi-Fi chipset and driver and Microsoft for Windows software.

Expanded support for Live Protect: Live Protect reduces the gap between vulnerability disclosure and patch completion on supported Cisco platforms and releases. Live Protect is now supported on N9000 Series Switches, N9300 Smart Switches, Catalyst SD-WAN, C9000 Series Smart Switches, and CW9800 Wireless Controllers. Support on Cisco 8000 Secure Routers and Cisco Firewalls is intended to be available by the end of 2026.

Privileged infrastructure access: Being developed in collaboration with Teleport, Cisco Privileged Infrastructure Access gives network teams and AI agents fast, governed, task-specific access to Cisco routers and switches, with short-lived, identity-bound certificates. Amy Coleman, Executive Vice President and Chief People Officer, shared the below communication with Microsoft employees today.

Today, we’re introducing a new Voluntary Exit Offer (VEO) to eligible employees within participating organizations. This offer gives eligible employees who may be considering a future outside the company a new choice to make that transition now with support. It also gives participating organizations another way to adapt their workforce to changing needs.

The Voluntary Exit Offer reflects an important part of how we’re evolving our approach to change: creating greater flexibility and, where possible, more ways for employees to shape their next chapter. This builds on what we learned earlier this year through the Voluntary Retirement Program.

What employees should know

This offer will be available to eligible employees in participating teams in Canada, India, the United Kingdom and the United States at level 70 and below. This is a time-limited, voluntary program that gives those who are eligible the opportunity to leave Microsoft with financial support and career planning resources. Some organizations are providing the Voluntary Exit Offer, and some are not. Participation varies based on each business’s priorities, customer commitments and workforce needs.

Eligible employees will receive an email with a link to their Voluntary Exit Offer details within the next few hours.

Looking ahead

The Voluntary Exit Offer is new for us. We’ll learn from it. At the same time, we’ll keep helping people focus on the work that matters most, build new skills and, where it makes sense, find new opportunities across Microsoft. There is no one-size-fits-all approach for every team or every employee. These are a few of the ways we’re trying to meet different business needs while continuing to create opportunities for our own people to grow and contribute.

My promise is to continue to provide clarity, listen and learn and keep improving.

Thank you for everything you continue to do for our customers, Microsoft and for one another.

Amy
